779--- ### Constructors with Multiple Parameters (Tuple Types)
780-
781-namespace Playground
782-
783--- A single constructor of an inductive type can have multiple parameters, not
784--- just zero or one. This feature is one way to define *tuple types* in Lean,
785--- which are like record/struct types but their fields are accessed by their
786--- *position* in patterns rather than by a specific (field) *name*.
787-
788--- As an example, consider representing the four bits in a nibble (half a
789--- byte). We first define a datatype `Bit` that resembles `Bool` (using the
790--- constructors `b1` and `b0` for the two possible bit values) and then define
791--- the datatype `Nibble`, which is a tuple of four bits.
792-
793-inductive Bit : Type where
794-  | b1
795-  | b0
796-
797-inductive Nibble : Type where
798-  | bits (x0 x1 x2 x3 : Bit)
799-
800-#check Nibble.bits .b1 .b0 .b1 .b0
801-
802--- Nibble.bits Bit.b1 Bit.b0 Bit.b1 Bit.b0 : Nibble
803-
804--- The `bits` constructor illustrates a feature of multi-parameter
805--- declarations, both for constructors and for functions: Instead of writing
806--- `(x0 : Bit) (x1 : Bit) ...` we write `(x0 x1 ... : Bit)` since all of the
807--- variables have the same type. We could have done the same with the function
808--- definition `MyBool.or` above, writing `or (b1 b2 : MyBool)` rather than
809--- `or (b1 : MyBool) (b2 : MyBool)`.
810-
811--- The `bits` constructor acts as a wrapper for its contents. Unwrapping is
812--- done by pattern matching, as in the `allZero` function below, which tests a
813--- Nibble to see if all its bits are `b0`.
814-
815-def allZero (nb : Nibble) : Bool :=
816-  match nb with
817-  | .bits .b0 .b0 .b0 .b0 => true
818-  | .bits _   _   _   _   => false
819-
820-example : allZero (.bits .b1 .b0 .b1 .b0) = false := by rfl
821-example : allZero (.bits .b0 .b0 .b0 .b0) = true  := by rfl
822-
823-end Playground
824-
825--- #### Structures
826-
827--- When defining an inductive type with just one constructor, we can instead
828--- use a `structure`:
829-
830-structure NibbleStruct : Type where
831-  x0 : Playground.Bit
832-  x1 : Playground.Bit
833-  x2 : Playground.Bit
834-  x3 : Playground.Bit
835-
836--- Rather than construct this as `.bits .b0 .b0 .b0 .b0`, we construct it as:
837-
838-#check NibbleStruct.mk .b0 .b0 .b0 .b0
839-
840--- { x0 := Playground.Bit.b0, x1 := Playground.Bit.b0, x2 := Playground.Bit.b0, x3 := Playground.Bit.b0 } : NibbleStruct
841-
842--- The `.mk` constructor is created for us. Structures are more commonly
843--- constructed by assigning values to their *fields*. Each field name is
844--- paired with its value using `:=`:
845-
846-def zeroNibble : NibbleStruct := {
847-    x0 := .b0
848-    x1 := .b0
849-    x2 := .b0
850-    x3 := .b0
851-  }
852-
853--- Since the result type is declared to be `NibbleStruct`, Lean knows which
854--- structure and fields we mean. Unlike `NibbleStruct.mk`, this construction
855--- syntax doesn't depend on the order of fields.
856-
857--- Now that we have seen how to construct a structure from scratch — how do we
858--- "update" an existing structure, or in other words, construct a new
859--- structure while reusing some old fields?
860-
861-def setFirstTwoBits (old : NibbleStruct)
862-    (newX0 : Playground.Bit)
863-    (newX1 : Playground.Bit) : NibbleStruct :=
864-  { old with x0 := newX0, x1 := newX1 }
865-
866--- The expression `{ old with ... }` constructs a new `NibbleStruct` whose
867--- `x0` and `x1` have the given value and whose other fields are copied from
868--- `old`. Keep in mind that `old` was not modified — we constructed a new
869--- structure starting from the old one.
870-
871-def makeNibbleStruct (x0 x1 x2 x3 : Playground.Bit) : NibbleStruct :=
872-  { x0, x1, x2, x3 }
873-
874--- When a field and the variable supplying its value have the same name, Lean
875--- lets us write just the name. Thus `{ x0, x1, x2, x3 }` is a shorthand for
876--- `{ x0 := x0, x1 := x1, x2 := x2, x3 := x3 }`. This is called *field
877--- abbreviation*.
878-
879--- ### Natural Numbers
880-
881--- We put this portion of the chapter in a namespace so that our definition of
882--- numbers does not interfere with the one from the standard library. Our
883--- definition matches the standard one, which we will use in the rest of the
884--- book.
885-
886-namespace NatPlayground
887-
888--- All the types we have defined so far — both enumerated types such as `Day`,
889--- `MyBool`, and `Playground.Bit` and tuple types such as `Playground.Nibble`
890--- built from them — are finite. The natural numbers, on the other hand, are
891--- an infinite set, so we'll need to use a slightly richer form of inductive
892--- type declaration to represent them: *recursive* inductive types.
893-
894--- While the need for recursion is unequivocal, there are many
895--- recursively-defined representations of numbers to choose from. You are
896--- certainly familiar with decimal notation (base 10), using the digits 0
897--- through 9, for example, to form the number 123. You have likely also
898--- encountered hexadecimal notation (base 16), in which the same number is
899--- represented as 7B, or octal (base 8), where it is 173, or binary (base 2),
900--- where it is 1111011. Using an enumerated type to represent digits, we could
901--- use any of these as our representation of natural numbers.
902-
903--- There are circumstances in which each of these choices is useful. The
904--- binary representation is valuable in computer hardware because the digits
905--- can be represented with just two distinct voltage levels, resulting in
906--- simple circuitry.
907-
908--- Here we choose an even simpler *unary* (base 1) representation, for the
909--- sake of streamlining proofs. As a Lean datatype, it uses two constructors.
910--- The `zero` constructor represents the number zero. The `succ` constructor
911--- can be applied to the representation of the natural number `n`, yielding
912--- the representation of `n + 1`, where `succ` stands for "successor." The
913--- number `n` is then represented by `n` applications of `succ` to `zero`.
914-
915--- Here is the complete datatype definition:
916-
917-inductive Nat : Type where
918-  | zero
919-  | succ (n : Nat)
920-
921--- With a little Lean magic, we can also arrange that ordinary numerals such
922--- as 0, 1, and 2 will be interpreted as values of our new `Nat` type whenever
923--- this is sensible in context.
924-
925--- The technical details of how this is done are not important for present
926--- purposes, so we won't spend time explaining them here. Instead, we'll mark
927--- them with `THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED` comments in `.lean` files and hide
928--- them in a collapsed text segment in the HTML presentation. Click on the
929--- triangle in the HTML if you want to have a look.
930-
931--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Library Nat to SFL Nat coercion
932-
933-def ofNat : _root_.Nat → Nat
934-  | .zero => .zero
935-  | .succ n => .succ (ofNat n)
936-
937-instance (n : _root_.Nat) : OfNat Nat n := ⟨ofNat n⟩
938-
939--- END DETAILS
940-
941--- We'll define some shorthands for numbers, putting them in the `Nat`
942--- namespace so we don't need to use `.` notation everywhere.
943-
944-namespace Nat
945-
946-def one   : Nat := succ zero
947-def two   : Nat := succ one
948-def three : Nat := succ two
949-def four  : Nat := succ three
950-
951--- We can also write functions on `Nat`.
952-
953-def pred (n : Nat) : Nat :=
954-  match n with
955-  | zero => zero
956-  | succ n' => n'
957-
958-def minusTwo (n : Nat) : Nat :=
959-  match n with
960-  | zero => zero
961-  | succ (zero) => zero
962-  | succ (succ n') => n'
963-
964-#eval minusTwo four
965-
966--- Look the types of `succ`, `pred`, and `minusTwo`:
967-
968-#check (succ)
969-#check (pred)
970-#check (minusTwo)
971-
972--- succ : Nat → Nat
973-
974--- pred : Nat → Nat
975-
976--- minusTwo : Nat → Nat
977-
978--- These are all things that can be applied to a number to yield a number.
979--- However, there is a fundamental difference between `succ` and the other
980--- two: functions like `pred` and `minusTwo` are defined by giving
981--- *computation rules* — e.g., the definition of `pred` says that
982--- `pred (succ (succ zero))` can be simplified to `succ zero` — while the
983--- definition of `succ` has no such behavior attached. Although it is like a
984--- function in the sense that it can be applied to an argument, it does not
985--- *do* anything at all! It is just the way we write down numbers.
986-
987--- We can also define *recursive functions*: functions that call themselves
988--- repeatedly down to a base case. Recursion is the essence of repeated
989--- computation in functional programming; in this course, we will make
990--- extensive use of recursive functions.
991-
992--- We first define a simple recursive function, `even`, then a slightly more
993--- sophisticated recursive function `add`.
994-
995-def even (n : Nat) : Bool :=
996-  match n with
997-  | zero => true
998-  | succ (zero) => false
999-  | succ (succ n') => even n'
1000-
1001-example : even one = false := by rfl
1002-example : even four = true := by rfl
1003-
1004--- We could define `odd` by a similar recursive declaration, but here is a
1005--- simpler way:
1006-
1007-def odd (n : Nat) : Bool :=
1008-  not (even n)
1009-
1010-example : odd one = true := by rfl
1011-example : odd four = false := by rfl
1012-
1013--- This function takes multiple parameters, recursing on the second:
1014-
1015-def add (n : Nat) (m : Nat) : Nat :=
1016-  match m with
1017-  | zero => n
1018-  | succ m' => succ (add n m')
1019-
1020-#eval add one two -- succ (succ (succ zero)) -- aka, three!
1021-
1022--- NatPlayground.Nat.succ (NatPlayground.Nat.succ (NatPlayground.Nat.succ (NatPlayground.Nat.zero)))
1023-
1024--- We can also define infix notation for our `add` functions.
1025-
1026--- Don't worry too much about how this is defined; we will return to it in
1027--- more detail later.
1028-
1029-scoped infixl:65 " + " => add
1030-
1031-#eval one + two -- succ (succ (succ zero)) -- aka, three again.
1032-
1033--- NatPlayground.Nat.succ (NatPlayground.Nat.succ (NatPlayground.Nat.succ (NatPlayground.Nat.zero)))
1034-
1035--- ## Proof by Rewriting
1036-
1037--- ### Proving properties about functions in Lean
1038-
1039--- Being recursive on a `Nat` and returning `Nat` as well, `add` is the first
1040--- example of a more sophisticated class of functions. In this chapter and
1041--- beyond, we will *prove* properties about recursive functions like `add`
1042--- over inductive datatypes like `Nat`, using *simplification rules*, also
1043--- known as *characterizing lemmas*, about their behavior.
1044-
1045--- Here is a simplification rule about `add`:
1046-
1047--- - `n + zero = n`
1048-
1049--- In Lean, this rule looks like this:
1050-
1051-theorem add_zero : ∀ n : Nat, n + zero = n := by
1052-  intro n
1053-  rfl
1054-
1055-#check add_zero
1056-
1057--- NatPlayground.Nat.add_zero (n : Nat) : n + zero = n
1058-
1059--- Using our simplification rule `add_zero`, we can carry out a simple proof
1060--- about natural numbers.
1061-
1062-theorem add_zero_zero : ∀ n : Nat, n + zero + zero = n := by
1063-  intro n
1064-  rewrite [add_zero]
1065-  rewrite [add_zero]
1066-  rfl
1067-
1068--- We'll walk through this proof in the next section.
1069-
1070--- ### Proof state and tactics
1071-
1072--- The `rewrite` tactic in the proof of `add_zero_zero` is used to transform
1073--- the goal of the proof according to an equality. The `add_zero` in brackets
1074--- is an *argument* to the `rewrite` tactic.
1075-
1076--- Let's walk through the theorem again in detail.
1077-
1078-theorem add_zero_zero_explained : ∀  n : Nat, n + zero + zero = n := by
1079-  intro n
1080-  /- After introducing `n`, our goal is `n + zero + zero = n`.
1081-     What can we do to simplify this expression? If you hover
1082-     your cursor over the `add_zero` in the rewrite below, you
1083-     can see its type: `n + zero = n`. So, we can use that
1084-     rewrite rule to transform an appearance of `n + zero`
1085-     in the goal to `n`. -/
1086-  rewrite [add_zero]
1087-  /- Now click here to see the new proof state that results
1088-     from the tactic. Notice how `n + zero + zero` changes to
1089-     `n + zero` in the goal. -/
1090-  rewrite [add_zero]
1091-  /- Again the goal changes, from `n + zero` to `n`. Now the
1092-     proof state is an equality with both sides equal, so it
1093-     can be closed by the tactic `rfl`. -/
1094-  rfl
1095-  /- The proof is now done! The Lean InfoView tells us there are
1096-     "No goals". -/
1097-
1098--- Give this proof a try (it's similar):
1099-
1100-theorem add_zero_zero_zero : ∀ n : Nat, n + zero + zero + zero = n := by
1101-  sorry
1102-
1103--- ### The `rewrite` tactic
1104-
1105--- The `rewrite` tactic tells Lean to rewrite (part of) a goal or hypothesis
1106--- based on a rule (or rules), given in square brackets. For example, given
1107--- the rule `add_zero`, which states that `n + zero` is equal to `n` for any
1108--- `n`, we can replace any `n + zero` in our proof with `n` via
1109--- `rewrite [add_zero]`.
1110-
1111--- ### The `rfl` tactic
1112-
1113--- The `rfl` tactic closes a goal of the shape `a = a`, for any `a`. It checks
1114--- that both sides of the equality are *definitionally equal* — that is, that
1115--- they reduce to the same term. (So, in particular, a term is always
1116--- definitionally equal to itself.)
1117-
1118--- ### A New `add` Rule
1119-
1120--- Here is another fundamental rule about addition:
1121-
1122--- `n + (succ m) = succ (n + m)`.
1123-
1124--- This is the rule we need to push `succ` around.
1125-
1126--- Here it is in Lean:
1127-
1128-theorem add_succ : ∀ n m : Nat, n + (succ m) = succ (n + m) := by
1129-  intro n m
1130-  rfl
1131-
1132--- Now, let's use `add_succ` in a proof:
1133-
1134-theorem add_one (n : Nat) : n + (succ zero) = succ n + zero := by
1135-  rewrite [add_succ]
1136-  rewrite [add_zero]
1137-  rewrite [add_zero]
1138-  rfl
1139-
1140--- We recommend stepping through these proofs in VS Code — that is, moving
1141--- past each tactic with your cursor to see how it changes the proof state and
1142--- hovering over each argument to `rewrite` to see its type.
1143-
1144--- ### Irreducibility, Rewriting, and Proof Engineering
1145-
1146--- Lean, like any other programming language, has conventions and best
1147--- practices for writing good software. Lean takes inspiration from
1148--- object-oriented programming in favoring the use of *encapsulation*. In OOP,
1149--- it is considered poor style to expose the fields of an object in its
1150--- interface; instead, those fields should only be accessible by an object's
1151--- methods (like getters and setters). Doing so hides the object's definition,
1152--- so that, if its fields or implementation ever change, the interface it
1153--- exposes to the outside world remains the same. In simple examples such
1154--- conventions may seem trivial or even silly; in complex codebases, it is the
1155--- only way to maintain crucial invariants that prevent a system from becoming
1156--- unmaintainable.
1157-
1158--- The same principle applies to programs and proofs in Lean. In idiomatic
1159--- Lean, it is considered poor style to *unfold* — that is, "peek through" —
1160--- definitions by using `rfl` to implicitly simplify expressions that aren't
1161--- syntactically identical. If you take a look at the proofs of `add_zero` and
1162--- `add_succ` above, you will notice this is exactly what we did when we used
1163--- the `rfl` tactic.
1164-
1165--- Fortunately, the foundational theorems `add_zero` and `add_succ` provide a
1166--- characterization of the behavior of `add` that makes using `rfl` to
1167--- simplify expressions unnecessary; instead, we can rewrite by these theorems
1168--- anywhere we want to describe how `add` evaluates. In real-world Lean
1169--- developments, the style of writing proofs using simplification rules is
1170--- both standard and expected.
1171-
1172--- For the next few chapters, we mark definitions with
1173--- `attribute [irreducible]` to prevent this peeking, also called
1174--- **definitional equality abuse** (**defeq abuse**, for short). We place this
1175--- attribute after the proofs of `add_zero` and `add_succ`, and can then
1176--- rewrite by these theorems anywhere we want to describe how `add` evaluates.
1177--- We use `attribute [irreducible]` for now to enforce the style of using
1178--- simplification rules, so that it is natural to you moving forward. We will
1179--- relax this discipline in later chapters.
1180-
1181-attribute [irreducible] add
1182-
1183--- These simplification rules also follow a particular pattern. Let's look
1184--- again at the definition of `add`, without the `+` notation for maximum
1185--- clarity:
1186-
1187-namespace AddPlayground
1188-
1189-def add (n : Nat) (m : Nat) : Nat :=
1190-  match m with
1191-  | zero => n
1192-  | succ m' => succ (add n m')
1193-
1194-theorem add_zero : ∀ (n : Nat), add n zero = n := by
1195-  intro n
1196-  rfl
1197-
1198-theorem add_succ : ∀ (n m : Nat), add n (succ m) = succ (add n m) := by
1199-  intro n m
1200-  rfl
1201-
1202-end AddPlayground
1203-
1204--- Each of `add_zero` and `add_succ` correspond to one branch of the `match`
1205--- statement defining `add` and describe how the evaluation of `add` proceeds
1206--- in that case. The `add_zero` theorem describes how `add n zero` evaluates,
1207--- while `add_succ` describes (symbolically) how `add n (succ m)` evaluates.
1208-
1209--- These are instances of a general pattern: each definition operating over
1210--- enumerated types like `Nat`, `Bool`, `Day`, or `Color` needs a
1211--- simplification rule for each branch of control flow through the function.
1212-
1213--- So, for example, we need two simplification rules for the definition of
1214--- `pred`:
1215-
1216-theorem pred_zero : pred zero = zero := by rfl
1217-theorem pred_succ n : pred (succ n) = n := by rfl
1218-
1219--- Now that we have defined and proved `pred`'s simplification rules, we can
1220--- mark it `irreducible`, to enforce rewriting by these lemmas.
1221-
1222-attribute [irreducible] pred
1223-
1224--- Similarly, for each of the three branches of the definition of `even`, we
1225--- need one simplification rule:
1226-
1227-theorem even_zero : even zero = true := rfl
1228-theorem even_one : even (succ zero) = false := rfl
1229-theorem even_succ_succ n : even (succ (succ n)) = even n := rfl
1230-
1231-attribute [irreducible] even odd
1232-
1233--- In the remainder of this textbook, we will pair definitions with
1234--- simplification rules. After proving these rules, instead of using `rfl` to
1235--- peek through the definitions, we will `rewrite` using the rules.
1236-
1237--- Eventually, we will introduce a way to *automatically* apply these
1238--- simplification rules. Real-world Lean developments use automation
1239--- extensively, and you will learn to do so gradually throughout this book.
1240--- For the moment it is important that you work through these early concepts
1241--- by hand, without automation. By the time the more powerful tools are
1242--- introduced, you will have the foundational understanding to use them with
1243--- precision and skill.
1244-

1335--- #### Equality and Ordering
1336-
1337--- When we say that Lean relies on almost nothing that's truly built-in, we
1338--- really mean it: even testing equality is not a primitive operation, but an
1339--- ordinary function that we could re-implement ourselves as users.
1340-
1341--- Here is a function `beq` that tests natural numbers for equality, yielding
1342--- a boolean.
1343-
1344-def beq (n m : Nat) : Bool :=
1345-  match n with
1346-  | zero => match m with
1347-            | zero => true
1348-            | succ _ => false
1349-  | succ n' => match m with
1350-               | zero => false
1351-               | succ m' => beq n' m'
1352-
1353--- We could also write this by pattern matching on both `n` and `m` at the
1354--- same time:
1355-
1356-def beq' (n m : Nat) : Bool :=
1357-  match n, m with
1358-  | zero, zero => true
1359-  | zero, succ _ => false
1360-  | succ _, zero => false
1361-  | succ n', succ m' => beq n' m'
1362-
1363--- The definitions of `beq` and `beq'` are equivalent.
1364-
1365--- Similarly, the `ble` function tests whether its first argument is less than
1366--- or equal to its second argument, yielding a boolean.
1367-
1368-def ble (n m : Nat) : Bool :=
1369-  match n with
1370-  | zero => true
1371-  | succ n' =>
1372-      match m with
1373-      | zero => false
1374-      | succ m' => ble n' m'
1375-
1376-theorem zero_ble (n : Nat) : ble zero n = true := by rfl
1377-theorem succ_ble_zero (n : Nat) : ble (succ n) zero = false := by rfl
1378-theorem succ_ble_succ (n m : Nat) : ble (succ n) (succ m) = ble n m := by rfl
1379-
1380-example : ble two two = true  := by rfl
1381-example : ble two four = true := by rfl
1382-example : ble four two = false := by rfl

1400--- We now have seen two symbols that both look like equality: `=` and `==`.
1401--- We'll have much more to say about their differences and similarities later.
1402--- For now, notice that `x = y` is a logical *claim* — a "proposition" — that
1403--- we can try to prove, while `x == y` is a boolean *expression* whose value
1404--- (either `true` or `false`) Lean can compute.

1417--- ### General Proofs about Natural Numbers
1418-
1419--- We now begin to make claims about *general* natural numbers.
1420-
1421--- We begin by making a universal claim about all numbers `n` and `m` that are
1422--- equal to each other (`n = m`). The arrow symbol is pronounced "implies."
1423--- Enter it with `\to` or `\->` or `\r`.
1424-
1425--- The `intro` tactic moves the universally quantified variables and the
1426--- hypothesis into the context, giving them names. The goal is now to prove
1427--- `n + n = m + m` under the assumption `h : n = m`.
1428-
1429--- The tactic that tells Lean to perform replacement is one we have seen
1430--- before: `rewrite`. It can take a hypothesis from the context as an
1431--- argument, just like it can take a previously proved theorem. In this case,
1432--- we want to rewrite with the hypothesis `h`, which says that `n` and `m` are
1433--- equal, so that we can replace `n` with `m` in the goal.
1434-
1435--- After the rewrite, the goal is `m + m = m + m`, which can be closed by
1436--- `rfl`.
1437-
1438-theorem add_id_example : ∀ n m : Nat,
1439-    n = m → n + n = m + m := by
1440-  intro n m
1441-  intro h
1442-  rewrite [h]
1443-  rfl
1444-

1453--- #### Displaying Theorem Statements
1454-
1455--- The `#check` command can also be used to examine the statements of
1456--- previously declared lemmas and theorems.
1457-
1458-#check mul_zero  -- ∀ (n : Nat), n * 0 = 0
1459-#check mul_succ  -- ∀ (n m : Nat), n * Nat.succ m = n + n * m
1460-
1461--- NatPlayground.Nat.mul_zero (n : Nat) : n * zero = zero
1462-
1463--- NatPlayground.Nat.mul_succ (n m : Nat) : n * succ m = n * m + n
1464-
1465--- Note that you may see a slight discrepancy in the output: `#check` shows
1466--- the theorem differently from the way it was introduced earlier.
1467-
1468--- First, Lean may print the theorem's fully qualified name
1469--- `NatPlayground.Nat.mul_zero`. The qualification identifies the namespace
1470--- containing the theorem, though the shorter name `mul_zero` is usually
1471--- sufficient when Lean can determine which declaration we mean.
1472-
1473--- Second, Lean displays the theorem's arguments before the colon
1474--- `mul_zero (n : Nat) : n * zero = zero`. Writing arguments as binders before
1475--- the colon is called *declaration-header style*. The same statement can be
1476--- written using an explicit universal quantifier, as we have seen before:
1477-
1478---   mul_zero : ∀ (n : Nat), n * zero = zero
1479-
1480--- Writing statements in declaration-header style shortens proofs because Lean
1481--- automatically adds declared variables to the context, rather than requiring
1482--- them to be added with `intro`. The declaration-header style is conventional
1483--- in Lean, and we will generally use it from now on.
1484-
1485--- ## Proof by Case Analysis
1486-
1487--- Of course, not everything can be proved by simple calculation and
1488--- rewriting: In general, the presence of unknown, hypothetical values
1489--- (arbitrary numbers, booleans, etc.) can block a proof.
1490-
1491-sf_expect_failure
1492-  example (n : Nat) : (succ n == zero) = false := by
1493-    /-
1494-      We can't rewrite by any lemmas here because `n` is unknown!
1495-    -/
1496-
1497--- The tactic that tells Lean to consider separate cases is called `cases`.
1498-
1499-theorem add_one_neb_zero (n : Nat) : (succ n == zero) = false := by
1500-  cases n with
1501-  | zero =>
1502-    rewrite [succ_zero_beq_false]
1503-    rfl
1504-  | succ n' =>
1505-    rewrite [succ_zero_beq_false]
1506-    rfl
1507-
1508--- The `cases` tactic generates *two* subgoals, which we must prove,
1509--- separately, in order to get Lean to accept the theorem. The generated
1510--- subgoals are tagged by the names of the constructors. `| zero =>` and
1511--- `| succ n' =>` select which subgoal to work on next and introduce variable
1512--- names. Note also that when we enter a subcase, we increase the level of
1513--- indentation at which we are working by two spaces.
1514-
1515--- The `cases` tactic can be used with any inductively defined datatype. For
1516--- example, we use it next to prove that boolean negation is involutive (that
1517--- is, that negation is its own inverse).
1518-
1519-theorem not_involutive (b : Bool) : (!!b) = b := by
1520-  cases b with
1521-  | false =>
1522-    rewrite [Bool.not_false, Bool.not_true]
1523-    rfl
1524-  | true =>
1525-    rewrite [Bool.not_true, Bool.not_false]
1526-    rfl
1527-
1528--- You may also notice that in the above proof we have used some rewrite rules
1529--- that we didn't previously prove in this file! These proofs come from Lean's
1530--- standard library, in particular from the section about booleans. Having
1531--- access to these already-proved theorems about booleans instead of needing
1532--- them to prove them ourselves is a big advantage of using Lean's built-in
1533--- `Bool` type instead of defining our own.
1534-
1535--- In a few chapters we will discuss how to search through the standard
1536--- library for theorems like these. For now, note that if you hover over the
1537--- name of these theorems in VSCode, the Lean 4 extension will show you their
1538--- type, i.e., what the theorem proves.
1539-
1540--- We can also have nested case analysis:
1541-
1542-theorem and_commutative (b c : Bool) :
1543-    (b && c) = (c && b) := by
1544-  cases b with
1545-  | true =>
1546-    cases c with
1547-    | true =>
1548-      rewrite [Bool.and_self]
1549-      rfl
1550-    | false =>
1551-      rewrite [Bool.and_false, Bool.and_true]
1552-      rfl
1553-  | false =>
1554-    cases c with
1555-    | true =>
1556-      rewrite [Bool.and_true, Bool.and_false]
1557-      rfl
1558-    | false =>
1559-      rewrite [Bool.and_self]
1560-      rfl
1561-
1562-theorem and3_exchange (b c d : Bool) :
1563-    ((b && c) && d) = ((b && d) && c) := by
1564-  cases b with
1565-  | false =>
1566-    cases c with
1567-    | true =>
1568-      cases d with
1569-      | false =>
1570-        rewrite [Bool.and_true, Bool.and_self]
1571-        rfl
1572-      | true =>
1573-        rewrite [Bool.and_true]
1574-        rfl
1575-    | false =>
1576-      cases d with
1577-      | false =>
1578-        rewrite [Bool.and_self]
1579-        rfl
1580-      | true =>
1581-        rewrite [Bool.and_self, Bool.and_true]
1582-        rfl
1583-  | true =>
1584-    cases c with
1585-    | true =>
1586-      cases d with
1587-      | false =>
1588-        rewrite [Bool.and_self, Bool.and_false, Bool.and_true]
1589-        rfl
1590-      | true =>
1591-        rewrite [Bool.and_self]
1592-        rfl
1593-    | false =>
1594-      cases d with
1595-      | false =>
1596-        rewrite [Bool.and_false]
1597-        rfl
1598-      | true =>
1599-        rewrite [Bool.and_false, Bool.and_true, Bool.and_self]
1600-        rfl
1601-
1602--- As you can see, proofs by cases can become very verbose. We will introduce
1603--- some tactics for writing shorter proofs by case analysis in Tactics
1604--- chapter.

1606--- ### New Tactics: `rewrite ... at` and `exact`
1607-
1608--- Some new tactics will be useful for the exercises ahead.
1609-
1610--- The `rewrite ... at` tactic can be used to rewrite in a hypothesis instead
1611--- of the goal. For example, if `hp : p` is in the context and we have a rule
1612--- `h : p = q`, then `rewrite [hp] at h` changes the hypothesis to `h : q`.
1613-
1614--- The `exact` tactic closes a goal by providing the exact proof of the goal.
1615--- For example, if `hp : p` is in the context and the goal is `p`, then
1616--- `exact hp` closes the goal. You can also transform `hp` slightly when using
1617--- `exact`, and we will explain how when we get to an example that needs it.

1635--- ### More on Notation (Optional)
1636-
1637--- Lean has a very flexible notation system. Operators like `+` and `*` are
1638--- defined with specified precedence and associativity. For example, `+` has
1639--- precedence 65 and is left-associative, while `*` has precedence 70 and is
1640--- also left-associative. This means that `1 + 2 * 3 * 4` is parsed as
1641--- `1 + ((2 * 3) * 4)`.
1642-
1643--- You can define custom notation using the `notation`, `infixl`, `infixr`,
1644--- `prefix`, and `postfix` commands.
1645-
1646--- Lean handles notation scoping through namespaces and *type classes*. The
1647--- numeric literal `3` can be interpreted as `Nat`, `Int`, `Float`, etc.,
1648--- depending on the expected type, thanks to Lean's `OfNat` type class. We
1649--- will explain type classes in more detail in the Typeclasses chapter.
1650-
1651--- ### Structural Recursion (Optional)
1652-
1653--- Here is a copy of the definition of `even`:
1654-
1655-def even' (n : Nat) : Bool :=
1656-  match n with
1657-  | zero => true
1658-  | succ (zero) => false
1659-  | succ (succ n') => even' n'
1660-
1661--- When Lean checks this definition, it verifies that the recursion
1662--- terminates. Specifically, it checks that one of the parameters is
1663--- *structurally decreasing* — each recursive call made in the body of the
1664--- definition is made on an argument that is smaller than the original input.
1665--- In `even'` example above, the argument to the recursive call to `even'` is
1666--- the variable `n'`. Because of our pattern match, we know that `n` is equal
1667--- to `succ (succ n')`, and therefore that `n'` is smaller than `n`. This
1668--- makes `n'` an acceptable argument to `even'` for Lean's termination
1669--- checker, and so this recursive definition is accepted.
1670-
1671--- This requirement is a fundamental feature of Lean's design: In particular,
1672--- it guarantees that every function that can be defined in Lean will
1673--- terminate on all inputs. However, because Lean's termination analysis is
1674--- not always able to figure things out automatically, it is sometimes
1675--- necessary to provide hints or write functions in slightly different ways.
1676-
1677--- ### Exercise (2 stars): decreasing ⭐⭐
1678-
1679--- To get a concrete sense of how termination checking works in Lean, find a
1680--- way to write a sensible recursive definition (of a simple function on
1681--- numbers, say) that does actually terminate on all inputs, but that Lean
1682--- will reject because it cannot automatically prove termination.
1683-
1684--- ### Binary Numerals
1685-
1686--- ### Exercise (3 stars): binary ⭐⭐⭐
1687-
1688--- We can generalize our unary representation of natural numbers to the more
1689--- efficient binary representation by treating a binary number as a sequence
1690--- of constructors `b0` and `b1` (representing 0s and 1s), terminated by a
1691--- `z`.
1692-
1693--- For example:
1694-
1695--- decimal                binary   unary
1696---       0                     z   zero
1697---       1                  b1 z   succ zero
1698---       2             b0 (b1 z)   succ (succ zero)
1699---       3             b1 (b1 z)   succ (succ (succ zero))
1700---       4        b0 (b0 (b1 z))   succ (succ (succ (succ zero)))
1701---       5        b1 (b0 (b1 z))   succ (succ (succ (succ (succ zero))))
1702---       6        b0 (b1 (b1 z))   succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ zero)))))
1703---       7        b1 (b1 (b1 z))   succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ zero))))))
1704---       8   b0 (b0 (b0 (b1 z)))   succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ zero)))))))
1705-
1706--- Note that the low-order bit is on the left and the high-order bit is on the
1707--- right — the opposite of the way binary numbers are usually written. This
1708--- choice makes them easier to manipulate.
1709-
1710--- (Comprehension check: What unary numeral does `b0 z` represent?)
1711-
1712-inductive Bin : Type where
1713-  | z
1714-  | b0 (n : Bin)
1715-  | b1 (n : Bin)
1716-
1717-attribute [pp_nodot] Bin.b1 Bin.b0
1718-
1719-def incr (m : Bin) : Bin
1720-  := sorry
1721-
1722-def binToNat (m : Bin) : Nat
1723-  := sorry
1724-
1725-theorem incr_test1 : incr (.b1 .z) = .b0 (.b1 .z) := sorry
1726-theorem incr_test2 : incr (.b0 (.b1 .z)) = .b1 (.b1 .z) := sorry
1727-theorem incr_test3 : incr (.b1 (.b1 .z)) = .b0 (.b0 (.b1 .z)) := sorry
1728-
1729-theorem incr_z : incr .z = .b1 .z := sorry

1731-theorem incr_b1 (m : Bin) : incr (.b1 m) = .b0 (incr m) := sorry
1732-
1733-theorem binToNat_z : binToNat .z = zero := sorry

1735-theorem binToNat_b1 (m : Bin) : binToNat (.b1 m) = binToNat m * two + one := sorry
1736-
1737--- You may find your previous proofs of `zero_add_one`, `one_add_one`,
1738--- `zero_mul_two`, `one_mul_two`, and `two_mul_two` useful here.

1744-
1745-attribute [irreducible] incr binToNat

1782--- ### Airport Exercise
1783-
1784--- Now that we have learned some basic features of Lean, let's close the
1785--- chapter with an exercise that brings them together.
1786-
1787--- In this exercise, we will model part of a database storing information
1788--- about travelers passing through an airport. The database contains one entry
1789--- per traveler, recording information about where the traveler is in the
1790--- airport process and the contents of their current carry-on bag.
1791-
1792--- We will implement several operations on these entries, state intended
1793--- properties of the database's behavior, and prove that the implementation
1794--- satisfies them.
1795-
1796-namespace Airport
1797-
1798--- For simplicity, a carry-on bag either contains a prohibited item, such as a
1799--- liquid that exceeds the allowed limit, causing it to fail inspection, or
1800--- contains only ordinary items.
1801-
1802-inductive BagContent : Type where
1803-  | prohibited
1804-  | ordinary
1805-
1806--- After a traveler checks in, the database also records the result of the
1807--- most recent security screening of their carry-on bag.
1808-
1809-inductive ScreeningStatus : Type where
1810-  | notScreened
1811-  | cleared
1812-  | blocked
1813-
1814--- Next, we define the possible stages of the airport process a traveler can
1815--- inhabit:
1816-
1817--- - they have not yet purchased a ticket;
1818-
1819--- - they have a ticket but have not yet checked in;
1820-
1821--- - they have checked in, in which case the database also stores the screening
1822---   status of their carry-on bag.
1823-
1824--- We can represent these possible database entries directly with an inductive
1825--- type.
1826-
1827-inductive Traveler : Type where
1828-  | noTicket  (bagContent : BagContent)
1829-  | ticketed  (bagContent : BagContent)
1830-  | checkedIn (bagContent : BagContent) (screeningStatus : ScreeningStatus)
1831-
1832--- Buying a ticket changes a traveler with no ticket into a ticketed traveler.
1833--- If the traveler already has a ticket or has already checked in, nothing
1834--- changes.
1835-
1836--- ### Exercise (1 star): buyTicket ⭐
1837-
1838-def buyTicket (t : Traveler) : Traveler := sorry
1839-example : buyTicket (.noTicket .ordinary) = .ticketed .ordinary := sorry
1840-example : buyTicket (.checkedIn .prohibited .blocked) = .checkedIn .prohibited .blocked := sorry
1841-
1842--- Here are the simplification rules for `buyTicket`:
1843-
1844-theorem buyTicket_noTicket (bagContent : BagContent) :
1845-    buyTicket (.noTicket bagContent) = .ticketed bagContent := sorry
1846-
1847-theorem buyTicket_ticketed (bagContent : BagContent) :
1848-    buyTicket (.ticketed bagContent) = .ticketed bagContent := sorry
1849-
1850-theorem buyTicket_checkedIn (bagContent : BagContent)
1851-    (screeningStatus : ScreeningStatus) :
1852-    buyTicket (.checkedIn bagContent screeningStatus) = .checkedIn bagContent screeningStatus := sorry
1853-
1854-attribute [irreducible] buyTicket
1855-
1856--- The first property we will prove about our system is that purchasing a
1857--- ticket is an *idempotent* operation (i.e., performing it twice has the same
1858--- effect as performing it once).
1859-
1860--- ### Exercise (2 stars): buy_ticket_idempotent ⭐⭐
1861-
1862-theorem buyTicket_idempotent (t : Traveler) :
1863-    buyTicket (buyTicket t) = buyTicket t := by
1864-  sorry
1865-
1866--- A traveler can check in only after buying a ticket. Checking in records
1867--- that their carry-on bag still needs to be inspected. Calling `checkIn`
1868--- before buying a ticket or after already checking in does nothing.
1869-
1870--- ### Exercise (1 star): checkIn ⭐
1871-
1872-def checkIn (t : Traveler) : Traveler := sorry
1873-
1874-example : checkIn (.noTicket .ordinary) = .noTicket .ordinary := sorry
1875-example : checkIn (.ticketed .prohibited) = .checkedIn .prohibited .notScreened := sorry
1876-example : checkIn (.checkedIn .ordinary .cleared) = .checkedIn .ordinary .cleared := sorry
1877-
1878--- Again, we record one rewrite rule for each case:
1879-
1880-theorem checkIn_noTicket (bagContent : BagContent) :
1881-    checkIn (.noTicket bagContent) = .noTicket bagContent := sorry
1882-
1883-theorem checkIn_ticketed (bagContent : BagContent) :
1884-    checkIn (.ticketed bagContent) = .checkedIn bagContent .notScreened := sorry
1885-
1886-theorem checkIn_checkedIn (bagContent : BagContent)
1887-    (screeningStatus : ScreeningStatus) :
1888-    checkIn (.checkedIn bagContent screeningStatus) = .checkedIn bagContent screeningStatus := sorry
1889-
1890-attribute [irreducible] checkIn
1891-
1892--- A traveler who does not yet have a ticket can buy one and then check in.
1893--- After this, the traveler is checked in and their carry-on ba bag needs to
1894--- be screened.
1895-
1896--- ### Exercise (1 star): buy_ticket_then_check_in ⭐
1897-
1898-theorem buyTicket_then_checkIn (bagContent : BagContent) :
1899-    checkIn (buyTicket (.noTicket bagContent)) = .checkedIn bagContent .notScreened := by
1900-  sorry
1901-
1902--- Carry-on inspection happens only after check-in. A bag containing only
1903--- ordinary items is cleared, while a bag containing a prohibited item is
1904--- blocked. If the traveler has not checked in, `inspectBag` does nothing.
1905-
1906--- ### Exercise (1 star): inspectBag ⭐
1907-
1908--- Define `inspectBag`.
1909-
1910-def inspectBag (t : Traveler) : Traveler := sorry
1911-
1912-example : inspectBag (.ticketed .prohibited) = .ticketed .prohibited := sorry
1913-example : inspectBag (.checkedIn .ordinary .notScreened) = .checkedIn .ordinary .cleared := sorry
1914-example : inspectBag (.checkedIn .prohibited .notScreened) = .checkedIn .prohibited .blocked := sorry
1915-
1916--- Again, we record one characterization lemma for each case.
1917-
1918-theorem inspectBag_noTicket (bagContent : BagContent) :
1919-    inspectBag (.noTicket bagContent) = .noTicket bagContent := sorry
1920-
1921-theorem inspectBag_ticketed (bagContent : BagContent) :
1922-    inspectBag (.ticketed bagContent) = .ticketed bagContent := sorry
1923-
1924-theorem inspectBag_ordinary (screeningStatus : ScreeningStatus) :
1925-    inspectBag (.checkedIn .ordinary screeningStatus) = .checkedIn .ordinary .cleared := sorry
1926-
1927-theorem inspectBag_prohibited (screeningStatus : ScreeningStatus) :
1928-    inspectBag (.checkedIn .prohibited screeningStatus) = .checkedIn .prohibited .blocked := sorry
1929-
1930-attribute [irreducible] inspectBag
1931-
1932--- ### Exercise (2 stars): inspect_bag_idempotent ⭐⭐
1933-
1934--- Show that inspecting same unchanged carry-on bag twice has the same effect
1935--- as inspecting it once.
1936-
1937-theorem inspectBag_idempotent (t : Traveler) : inspectBag (inspectBag t) = inspectBag t := by
1938-  sorry
1939-
1940--- A traveler may leave the screened area and return with a different carry-on
1941--- bag. Since the previous screening result applied to the old bag, a new
1942--- carry-on must be screened again before the traveler can re-enter.
1943-
1944--- ### Exercise (1 star): changeBag ⭐
1945-
1946--- Define `changeBag`.
1947-
1948-def changeBag (newContent : BagContent) (t : Traveler) : Traveler := sorry
1949-
1950-example : changeBag .prohibited (.ticketed .ordinary) = .ticketed .prohibited := sorry
1951-example : changeBag .prohibited (.checkedIn .ordinary .cleared) = .checkedIn .prohibited .notScreened := sorry
1952-
1953--- As before, we record the behavior of each case as a rewrite rule.
1954-
1955-theorem changeBag_noTicket (newContent oldContent : BagContent) :
1956-    changeBag newContent (.noTicket oldContent) = .noTicket newContent := sorry
1957-
1958-theorem changeBag_ticketed (newContent oldContent : BagContent) :
1959-    changeBag newContent (.ticketed oldContent) = .ticketed newContent := sorry
1960-
1961-theorem changeBag_checkedIn (newContent oldContent : BagContent)
1962-    (screeningStatus : ScreeningStatus) :
1963-    changeBag newContent (.checkedIn oldContent screeningStatus) =
1964-    .checkedIn newContent .notScreened := sorry
1965-
1966-attribute [irreducible] changeBag
1967-
1968--- It is easy to see that replacing a bag after it has been inspected resets
1969--- its screening status. In other words, `inspectBag` and `changeBag` do not,
1970--- in general, commute: the order in which the two operations are performed
1971--- can affect the result.
1972-
1973--- However, if the traveler has not checked in, `inspectBag` does nothing, so
1974--- changing and inspecting the carry-on can be performed in either order.
1975--- There are two such cases: the traveler may not yet have a ticket, or may
1976--- have a ticket but not yet be checked in.
1977-
1978--- ### Exercise (2 stars): inspect_changeBag_commute ⭐⭐
1979-
1980-theorem inspectBag_changeBag_comm_noTicket
1981-    (oldContent newContent : BagContent) :
1982-    inspectBag (changeBag newContent (.noTicket oldContent)) =
1983-    changeBag newContent (inspectBag (.noTicket oldContent)) := by
1984-  sorry
1985-
1986-theorem inspectBag_changeBag_comm_ticketed
1987-    (oldContent newContent : BagContent) :
1988-    inspectBag (changeBag newContent (.ticketed oldContent)) =
1989-    changeBag newContent (inspectBag (.ticketed oldContent)) := by
1990-  sorry
1991-
1992-end Airport
1993-

18-namespace Lean.Parser
19-open Tactic
20-
21-/-- Internal syntactic representation of a single inversion alternative. -/
22-declare_syntax_cat invAlt
23-syntax " | " caseArg " => " tacticSeq : invAlt
24-
25-/-- An inversion alternative matching one or more goal tags,
26-  expanding to multiple single [invAlt]s. -/
27-declare_syntax_cat invAlts
28-syntax (" | " caseArg)+ " => " tacticSeq : invAlts
29-
30-/--
31-  `inversion t` generalizes nonvariable indices of the type of `t` before invoking `cases t`,
32-  then solves away contradictory generated goals.
33-  `t` itself will also be generalized with a heterogeneous equality `heq`
34-  if trying to generalize the indices produces an ill-typed result.
35-  * If `inversion +clear t` is set, then `heq` will be `clear`ed from the context if present,
36-    along with `t` if there are no dependencies on it.
37-  * The form `inversion t with | tag₁ x ... => tac ... | ... | tagₙ z ... => tac ...` is supported,
38-    similar to that of `cases` and `inversion`.
39--/
40-syntax (name := inversion)
41-  "inversion " optConfig ident (" with " (colGe invAlts)+)? : tactic
42-
43-end Lean.Parser

45-namespace Lean.Meta
46-
47-/--
48-  This function is similar to `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`: Given `e` of the
49-  form `forall ..xs, A`, this combinator will create a new metavariable for
50-  each `x` in `xs` until it reaches an `x` whose type is defeq to `t`,
51-  and instantiate `A` with these, while also reducing `A` if needed.
52-  It uses `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`.
53-
54-  This function returns a triple `(mvs, bis, out)` where
55-  - `mvs` is an array containing the new metavariables.
56-  - `bis` is an array containing the binder infos for the `mvs`.
57-  - `out` is `e` but instantiated with the `mvs`.
58-
59-  Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Lean/Meta/Basic.lean#L41].
60--/
61-def forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq
62-    (e t : Expr) (kind : MetavarKind := MetavarKind.natural) :
63-    MetaM (Array Expr × Array BinderInfo × Expr) := do
64-  let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing e (some 1) kind
65-  unless ms.size == 1 do
66-    if ms.size == 0 then throwError m!"Failed: {← ppExpr e} is not the type of a function."
67-    else throwError m!"Failed"
68-  let mut mvs := ms
69-  let mut bis := bs
70-  let mut out : Expr := tp
71-  while !(← isDefEq (← inferType mvs.toList.getLast!) t) do
72-    let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing out (some 1) kind
73-    unless ms.size == 1 do
74-      throwError m!"Failed to find {← ppExpr t} as the type of a parameter of {← ppExpr e}."
75-    mvs := mvs ++ ms
76-    bis := bis ++ bs
77-    out := tp
78-  return (mvs, bis, out)
79-
80-/-- Get the user-facing name for the given metavariable. -/
81-def _root_.Lean.MVarId.getUserName (mvarId : MVarId) : MetaM Name := do
82-  let decl ← mvarId.getDecl
83-  return decl.userName
84-
85-/-- Given equations `eqs` in the local context of `mvarId`,
86-  unify them using [Lean.Meta.unifyEq?],
87-  but if unification fails, leave the equation in the context.
88-  This means we should never get a "Dependent elimination failed" error.
89-  While marked partial, this _should_ always terminate,
90-  decreasing on the sum of the sizes of the terms of each equation.
91-
92-  Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyEqs]. -/
93-partial def unifyEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (mvarId : MVarId) (subst : FVarSubst) (caseName? : Option Name) : MetaM (MVarId × FVarSubst) := withIncRecDepth do
94-  match eqs with
95-  | [] => return (mvarId, subst)
96-  | eq :: eqs =>
97-    let some { mvarId, subst, numNewEqs } ← Option.join <$> (observing? $ unifyEq? mvarId eq subst MVarId.acyclic caseName?)
98-      | unifyEqs eqs mvarId subst caseName?
99-    let (newEqs, mvarId) ← mvarId.introN numNewEqs
100-    let eqs := eqs.map (Expr.fvarId! ∘ subst.get)
101-    unifyEqs (newEqs.toList ++ eqs) mvarId subst caseName?
102-
103-/-- Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyCasesEqs]. -/
104-def unifyCasesEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
105-  subgoals.filterMapM fun s => do
106-    let eqs := eqs.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
107-    let (mvarId, subst) ← unifyEqs eqs s.mvarId s.subst s.ctorName
108-    if (← mvarId.isAssignedOrDelayedAssigned) then return none
109-    else return some { s with
110-      mvarId := mvarId,
111-      subst  := subst,
112-      fields := s.fields.map (subst.apply ·)
113-    }
114-
115-/-- Try to clear the given fvars from the local context of each subgoal,
116-  using the subgoals' substitution mappings to find the fvars.
117-
118-  As with [MVarId.tryClearMany], the fvars must be in the order they appear in the context.  -/
119-def casesClearMany (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) (fvarIds : Array FVarId) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
120-  subgoals.mapM fun s => do
121-    let fvarIds := fvarIds.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
122-    let mvarId ← s.mvarId.tryClearMany fvarIds
123-    return { s with mvarId }
124-
125-end Lean.Meta
126-
127-namespace Lean.Elab.Tactic
128-open Meta Term
129-
130--- [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Tactic/Lemma.lean]
131--- [https://github.com/leanprover-community/batteries/blob/main/Batteries/Tactic/Lemma.lean]
132-/-- Synonym for `theorem`. -/
133-macro "lemma " thm:declId sig:declSig val:declVal : command => `(theorem $thm $sig $val)
134-
135-/--
136-  `apply t at i` uses forward reasoning with `t` at the hypothesis `i`.
137-  Explicitly, if `t : α₁ → ⋯ → αᵢ → ⋯ → αₙ` and `i` has type `αᵢ`, then this tactic adds
138-  metavariables/goals for any terms of `αⱼ` for `j = 1, …, i-1`,
139-  then replaces the type of `i` with `αᵢ₊₁ → ⋯ → αₙ` by applying those metavariables and the
140-  original `i`.
141-
142-  Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Tactic/ApplyAt.lean].
143--/
144-elab "apply " t:term " at " i:ident : tactic => withSynthesize <| withMainContext do
145-  let f ← elabTermForApply t
146-  let some ldecl := (← getLCtx).findFromUserName? i.getId
147-    | throwErrorAt i m!"Identifier {i} not found"
148-  let (mvs, bis, _) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq (← inferType f) ldecl.type
149-  for (m, b) in mvs.zip bis do
150-    if b.isInstImplicit && !(← m.mvarId!.isAssigned) then
151-      try m.mvarId!.inferInstance
152-      catch _ => continue
153-  let (_, mainGoal) ← (← getMainGoal).note ldecl.userName
154-    (← mkAppOptM' f (mvs.pop.push ldecl.toExpr |>.map some))
155-  let mainGoal ← mainGoal.tryClear ldecl.fvarId
156-  replaceMainGoal <| [mainGoal] ++ mvs.pop.toList.map (·.mvarId!)
157-
158-structure InversionConfig where
159-  clear : Bool := false
160-
161-declare_config_elab elabInversionConfig InversionConfig
162-
163-open Cases in
164-def inversionCore (h : FVarId) (config : InversionConfig) : TacticM (List CasesSubgoal) := withMainContext do
165-  let goal ← getMainGoal
166-  goal.withContext do
167-    let some ctx ← mkCasesContext? h
168-    | throwTacticEx `inversion goal "Target {Expr.fvar h} does not belong to an inductive type"
169-    -- If the target's type isn't a predicate with indices, behave like `cases`
170-    if ← hasIndepIndices ctx then
171-      let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn goal h default ctx
172-      let subgoals ← if config.clear
173-        then casesClearMany subgoals #[h]
174-        else pure subgoals
175-      return subgoals.toList
176-    -- Otherwise, use custom [unifyEqs] to not fail on unifying HEqs
177-    else
178-      let gis@⟨newGoal, _, newTarget, numEqs⟩ ← generalizeIndices goal h
179-      let (newEqs, newGoal) ← newGoal.introN numEqs
180-      let some targetEq := newEqs.back?
181-      | throwTacticEx `inversion newGoal "Failed to generalize target"
182-      let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn newGoal newTarget default ctx
183-      let subgoals ← elimAuxIndices gis subgoals
184-      let subgoals ← unifyCasesEqs newEqs.toList subgoals
185-      let subgoals ← if config.clear
186-        then casesClearMany subgoals #[h, targetEq]
187-        else pure subgoals
188-      return subgoals.toList
189-
190-/-- Given an inversion alternative and a list of goals,
191-  solve the tagged goal with the provided tactics,
192-  throwing an error if the goal cannot be found or solved. -/
193-def evalInvAlt (goals : List CasesSubgoal) (alt : TSyntax `invAlt) : TacticM (List MVarId) :=
194-  match alt with
195-  | `(invAlt| | $tag:ident $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
196-    if let some goal := goals.find? (matchTag tag.getId $ ·.ctorName.getD default) then
197-      return [← trySolveGoal vars tactics goal.mvarId]
198-    else throwError m!"Invalid alternative name `{tag.getId}`: {← errorMsg}"
199-  | `(invAlt| | _ $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
200-    if !goals.isEmpty then
201-      goals.mapM (trySolveGoal vars tactics ·.mvarId)
202-    else throwErrorAt alt m!"Invalid wildcard alternative: {← errorMsg}"
203-  | _ => throwErrorAt alt "Could not parse inversion alternative"
204-where
205-  matchTag tag name : Bool :=
206-    tag == name || tag.isPrefixOf name || tag.isSuffixOf name
207-  trySolveGoal vars tactics goal : TacticM MVarId := do
208-    let goals ← renameInaccessibles goal vars >>= evalTacticAt tactics
209-    unless goals.isEmpty do
210-      reportUnsolvedGoals goals
211-    return goal
212-  errorMsg : TacticM MessageData := do
213-    let goalMsgs := goals.filterMap (.ofName <$> ·.ctorName)
214-    return if goals.isEmpty
215-      then m!"There are no unhandled alternatives"
216-      else m!"Expected {.orList goalMsgs}"
217-
218-@[tactic Lean.Parser.inversion, inherit_doc Lean.Parser.inversion]
219-public meta def evalInversion : Tactic
220-  | `(tactic| inversion $config $h:ident $[with $[$alts?:invAlts]*]?) => do
221-    let config ← elabInversionConfig config
222-    let mut goals ← inversionCore (← getFVarId h) config
223-    if let some alts := alts? then
224-      let expandedAlts ← Array.flatten <$> alts.mapM expandInvAlts
225-      for alt in expandedAlts do
226-        let solvedGoals ← evalInvAlt goals alt
227-        goals := goals.filter (!solvedGoals.contains ·.mvarId)
228-      unless goals.isEmpty do
229-        reportUnsolvedGoals $ goals.map (·.mvarId)
230-    replaceMainGoal $ goals.map (·.mvarId)
231-  | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion tactic"
232-where expandInvAlts
233-  | `(invAlts| $[| $args:caseArg]* => $tactics:tacticSeq) =>
234-    args.mapM (`(invAlt| | $(·) => $tactics))
235-  | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion alternatives"
236-
237-end Lean.Elab.Tactic

LF/IndProp.lean

1-import LF.Logic
2-import LF.CustomTactics
3-
4-import LF.SFLCompat
5-
6--- # IndProp: Inductively Defined Propositions
7-
8--- ## Inductively Defined Propositions
9-
10--- In the Logic chapter, we looked at several ways of writing propositions,
11--- including conjunction, disjunction, and existential quantification.
12-
13--- In this chapter, we bring yet another new tool into the mix: *inductively
14--- defined propositions*.
15-
16--- To begin, some examples...
17-
18--- ### Example: The Collatz Conjecture
19-
20--- The *Collatz Conjecture* is a famous open problem in number theory.
21-
22--- Its statement is quite simple. First, we define a function `csf` on
23--- numbers, as follows (where `csf` stands for "Collatz step function"):
24-
25-def div2 (n : Nat) : Nat :=
26-  match n with
27-  | 0      => 0
28-  | 1      => 0
29-  | n' + 2 => div2 n' + 1
30-
31-def csf (n : Nat) : Nat :=
32-  if n.even then div2 n
33-  else (3 * n) + 1
34-
35--- Next, we look at what happens when we repeatedly apply `csf` to some given
36--- starting number. For example, `csf 12` is `6`, and `csf 6` is `3`, so by
37--- repeatedly applying `csf` we get the sequence
38--- `12, 6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1`.
39-
40--- Similarly, if we start with `19`, we get the longer sequence
41--- `19,
42--- 58, 29, 88, 44, 22, 11, 34, 17, 52, 26, 13, 40, 20, 10, 5, 16, 8,
43--- 4, 2, 1`.
44-
45--- Both of these sequences eventually reach `1`. The question posed by Collatz
46--- was: Is the sequence starting from *any* positive natural number guaranteed
47--- to reach `1` eventually?
48-
49--- To formalize this question in Lean, we might try to define a recursive
50--- *function* that calculates the total number of steps that it takes for such
51--- a sequence to reach `1`. You can write this definition in a standard
52--- programming language, but it is rejected by Lean's termination checker,
53--- since the argument to the recursive call, `csf n`, is not "obviously
54--- smaller" than `n`.
55-
56-sf_expect_failure
57-  def reaches1In (n : Nat) : Nat :=
58-    if n == 1 then 0
59-    else 1 + reaches1In (csf n)
60-
61--- fail to show termination for
62---   reaches1In
63--- with errors
64--- failed to infer structural recursion:
65--- Cannot use parameter n:
66---   failed to eliminate recursive application
67---     reaches1In (csf n)
68-
69-
70--- failed to prove termination, possible solutions:
71---   - Use `have`-expressions to prove the remaining goals
72---   - Use `termination_by` to specify a different well-founded relation
73---   - Use `decreasing_by` to specify your own tactic for discharging this kind of goal
74--- n : Nat
75--- h✝ : ¬(n == 1) = true
76--- ⊢ csf n < n
77-
78--- Indeed, this isn't just a pointless limitation: functions in Lean are
79--- required to be total, to ensure logical consistency.
80-
81--- Moreover, we can't fix it by devising a more clever termination checker:
82--- deciding whether this particular function is total would be equivalent to
83--- settling the Collatz conjecture!
84-
85--- Another idea could be to express the concept "eventually reaches `1` in the
86--- Collatz sequence" as a *recursively defined property* of numbers
87--- `CollatzHoldsFor : Nat → Prop`. This is also rejected by the termination
88--- checker. In principle, we could convince Lean that `div2 n` is smaller than
89--- `n` by supplying an appropriate proof. However, we still can't convince it
90--- that `(3 * n) + 1` is smaller than `n`!
91-
92-sf_expect_failure
93-  def CollatzHoldsFor (n : Nat) : Prop :=
94-    match n with
95-    | 0 => False
96-    | 1 => True
97-    | _ => if n.even then CollatzHoldsFor (div2 n)
98-                     else CollatzHoldsFor ((3 * n) + 1)
99-
100--- fail to show termination for
101---   CollatzHoldsFor
102--- with errors
103--- failed to infer structural recursion:
104--- Cannot use parameter n:
105---   failed to eliminate recursive application
106---     CollatzHoldsFor (div2 n)
107-
108-
109--- failed to prove termination, possible solutions:
110---   - Use `have`-expressions to prove the remaining goals
111---   - Use `termination_by` to specify a different well-founded relation
112---   - Use `decreasing_by` to specify your own tactic for discharging this kind of goal
113--- n x✝ : Nat
114--- h✝ : n.even = true
115--- ⊢ div2 n < x✝
116-
117--- Fortunately, there is another way to do it: We can express the concept
118--- "reaches `1` eventually in the Collatz sequence" as an *inductively defined
119--- property* of numbers. Intuitively, this property is defined by a set of
120--- rules:
121-
122---                 ─────────────────── (chf_one)
123---                  CollatzHoldsFor 1
124-
125---   even n = true     CollatzHoldsFor (div2 n)
126---   ─────────────────────────────────────────── (chf_even)
127---                  CollatzHoldsFor n
128-
129---   even n = false    CollatzHoldsFor ((3 * n) + 1)
130---   ─────────────────────────────────────────────── (chf_odd)
131---                  CollatzHoldsFor n
132-
133--- So there are three ways to prove that a number `n` eventually reaches `1`
134--- in the Collatz sequence:
135-
136--- - `n` is `1`;
137--- - `n` is even and `div2 n` eventually reaches `1`;
138--- - `n` is odd and `(3 * n) + 1` eventually reaches `1`.
139-
140--- We can prove that a number reaches `1` by constructing a (finite)
141--- derivation using these rules. For instance, here is the derivation proving
142--- that `12` reaches `1` (where we leave out the evenness/oddness premises):
143-
144---   ─────────────────────── (chf_one)
145---     CollatzHoldsFor 1
146---   ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
147---     CollatzHoldsFor 2
148---   ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
149---     CollatzHoldsFor 4
150---   ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
151---     CollatzHoldsFor 8
152---   ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
153---     CollatzHoldsFor 16
154---   ─────────────────────── (chf_odd)
155---     CollatzHoldsFor 5
156---   ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
157---     CollatzHoldsFor 10
158---   ─────────────────────── (chf_odd)
159---     CollatzHoldsFor 3
160---   ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
161---     CollatzHoldsFor 6
162---   ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
163---     CollatzHoldsFor 12
164-
165--- Formally in Lean, the `CollatzHoldsFor` property is *inductively defined*:
166-
167-inductive CollatzHoldsFor : Nat → Prop where
168-  | chf_one  : CollatzHoldsFor 1
169-  | chf_even (n : Nat) : n.even = true →
170-                         CollatzHoldsFor (div2 n) →
171-                         CollatzHoldsFor n
172-  | chf_odd  (n : Nat) : n.even = false →
173-                         CollatzHoldsFor ((3 * n) + 1) →
174-                         CollatzHoldsFor n
175-
176--- What we've done here is to use Lean's `inductive` definition mechanism to
177--- characterize the property "Collatz holds for..." by stating three different
178--- ways in which it can hold: (1) Collatz holds for `1`, (2) if Collatz holds
179--- for `div2 n` and `n` is even then Collatz holds for `n`, and (3) if Collatz
180--- holds for `(3 * n) + 1` and `n` is odd then Collatz holds for `n`. This
181--- Lean definition directly corresponds to the three rules we wrote informally
182--- above.
183-
184--- For particular numbers, we can now prove that the Collatz sequence reaches
185--- `1` (we'll look more closely at how it works a bit later in the chapter).
186--- Each step applies a rule and discharges the boolean evenness premise by
187--- `rfl`; the recursive premise is then reduced by the kernel from
188--- `CollatzHoldsFor (div2 12)` to `CollatzHoldsFor 6`, etc.
189-
190-example : CollatzHoldsFor 12 := by
191-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
192-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
193-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_odd;   rfl
194-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
195-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_odd;   rfl
196-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
197-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
198-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
199-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
200-  exact CollatzHoldsFor.chf_one
201-
202--- The Collatz conjecture then states that the sequence beginning from *any*
203--- positive number reaches `1`:
204-
205-def Collatz := ∀ n, n ≠ 0 → CollatzHoldsFor n
206-
207--- If you succeed in proving this conjecture, you've got a bright future as a
208--- number theorist! But don't spend too long on it -- it's been open since
209--- 1937.
210-
211--- ### Example: Binary relation for comparing numbers
212-
213--- A binary *relation* on a set `α` has Lean type `α → α → Prop`. This is a
214--- family of propositions parameterized by two elements of `α` -- i.e., a
215--- proposition about pairs of elements of `α`.
216-
217--- For example, one familiar binary relation on `Nat` is
218--- `Le : Nat
219--- → Nat → Prop`, the less-than-or-equal-to relation, which can be
220--- inductively defined by the following two rules:
221-
222---     ─────── (le_refl)
223---     Le n n
224-
225---      Le n m
226---   ───────────── (le_step)
227---   Le n (m + 1)
228-
229--- These rules say that there are two ways to show that a number is less than
230--- or equal to another: either observe that they are the same number, or, if
231--- the second has the form `m + 1`, give evidence that the first is less than
232--- or equal to `m`.
233-
234-namespace LePlayground
235-
236-inductive Le : Nat → Nat → Prop where
237-  | refl (n : Nat)   : Le n n
238-  | step (n m : Nat) : Le n m → Le n (m + 1)
239-
240-scoped infix:50 (priority := high) " ≤ " => Le
241-
242--- This definition is a bit simpler and more elegant than the Boolean function
243--- `ble` we defined in `Basics`. As usual, `Le` and `ble` are equivalent, and
244--- there is an exercise about that later.
245-
246-example : 3 ≤ 5 := by
247-  apply Le.step; apply Le.step; exact Le.refl 3
248-
249-end LePlayground
250-
251--- ### Example: Transitive Closure
252-
253--- Another example: The *transitive closure* of a relation `R` is the smallest
254--- relation that contains `R` and that is transitive. This can be defined by
255--- the following two rules:
256-
257---                 R x y
258---            ─────────────── (t_step)
259---            ClosTrans R x y
260-
261---   ClosTrans R x y    ClosTrans R y z
262---   ──────────────────────────────────── (t_trans)
263---            ClosTrans R x z
264-
265--- In Lean this looks as follows:
266-
267-inductive ClosTrans {α : Type} (R : α → α → Prop) : α → α → Prop where
268-  | t_step (x y : α) :
269-      R x y →
270-      ClosTrans R x y
271-  | t_trans (x y z : α) :
272-      ClosTrans R x y →
273-      ClosTrans R y z →
274-      ClosTrans R x z
275-
276--- For example, suppose we define a "parent of" relation on a group of
277--- people...
278-
279-inductive Person : Type where
280-  | sage
281-  | cleo
282-  | ridley
283-  | moss
284-
285-inductive ParentOf : Person → Person → Prop where
286-  | po_SC : ParentOf .sage .cleo
287-  | po_SR : ParentOf .sage .ridley
288-  | po_CM : ParentOf .cleo .moss
289-
290--- In this example, `sage` is a parent of both `cleo` and `ridley`; and `cleo`
291--- is a parent of `moss`.
292-
293--- The `parent_of` relation is not transitive, but we can define an "ancestor
294--- of" relation as its transitive closure:
295-
296-def AncestorOf : Person → Person → Prop := ClosTrans ParentOf
297-
298--- Here is a derivation showing that Sage is an ancestor of Moss:
299-
300---    ———————————————————(po_SC)     ———————————————————(po_CM)
301---    ParentOf .sage .cleo            ParentOf .cleo .moss
302---   —————————————————————(t_step)  —————————————————————(t_step)
303---   AncestorOf .sage .cleo          AncestorOf .cleo .moss
304---   ————————————————————————————————————————————————————(t_trans)
305---                   AncestorOf .sage .moss
306-
307-example : AncestorOf .sage .moss := by
308-  apply ClosTrans.t_trans
309-  . apply ClosTrans.t_step; apply ParentOf.po_SC
310-  . apply ClosTrans.t_step; apply ParentOf.po_CM
311-
312--- Computing the transitive closure can be undecidable even for a relation R
313--- that is decidable (e.g., the `CMS` relation below), so in general we can't
314--- expect to define transitive closure as a boolean function. Fortunately,
315--- Lean allows us to define transitive closure as an inductive relation.
316-
317--- The transitive closure of a binary relation cannot, in general, be
318--- expressed in first-order logic. The logic of Lean is, however, much more
319--- powerful, and can easily define such inductive relations.
320-
321--- ### Example: Reflexive and Transitive Closure
322-
323--- As another example, the *reflexive and transitive closure* of a relation
324--- `R` is the smallest relation that contains `R` and that is reflexive and
325--- transitive. This can be defined by the following three rules (where we
326--- added a reflexivity rule to `ClosTrans`):
327-
328---                      R x y
329---            ——————————————————————— (rt_step)
330---              ClosReflTrans R x y
331-
332---            ——————————————————————— (rt_refl)
333---              ClosReflTrans R x x
334-
335---      ClosReflTrans R x y    ClosReflTrans R y z
336---   —————————————————————————————————————————————— (rt_trans)
337---              ClosReflTrans R x z
338-
339-inductive ClosReflTrans {α : Type} (R : α → α → Prop) : α → α → Prop where
340-  | rt_step (x y : α) :
341-      R x y →
342-      ClosReflTrans R x y
343-  | rt_refl (x : α) :
344-      ClosReflTrans R x x
345-  | rt_trans (x y z : α) :
346-      ClosReflTrans R x y →
347-      ClosReflTrans R y z →
348-      ClosReflTrans R x z
349-
350--- For instance, this enables an equivalent definition of the Collatz
351--- conjecture. First we define a binary relation corresponding to the "Collatz
352--- step function" `csf`:
353-
354-def CS (n m : Nat) : Prop := csf n = m
355-
356--- This Collatz step relation can be used in conjunction with the reflexive
357--- and transitive closure operation to define a *Collatz multi-step* (`CMS`)
358--- relation, expressing that a number `n` reaches another number `m` in zero
359--- or more Collatz steps:
360-
361-def CMS (n m : Nat) : Prop := ClosReflTrans CS n m
362-def Collatz' : Prop := ∀ (n : Nat), n ≠ 0 → CMS n 1
363-
364--- This `CMS` relation defined in terms of `ClosReflTrans` allows for more
365--- interesting derivations than the linear ones of the directly-defined
366--- `CollatzHoldsFor` relation:
367-
368---   csf 16 = 8           csf 8 = 4           csf 4 = 2           csf 2 = 1
369---   ——————————(rt_step)  —————————(rt_step)  —————————(rt_step)  —————————(rt_step)
370---   CMS 16 8           CMS 8 4           CMS 4 2           CMS 2 1
371---   ——————————————————————————(rt_trans)  —————————————————————————(rt_trans)
372---       CMS 16 4                              CMS 4 1
373---       —————————————————————————————————————————————(rt_trans)
374---                          CMS 16 1
375-
376--- ### Exercise (1 star): clos_refl_trans_sym (manually graded) ⭐
377-
378--- How would you modify the `ClosReflTrans` definition above so as to define
379--- the reflexive, symmetric, and transitive closure?
380-
381--- FILL IN HERE
382-
383--- ### Example: Permutations
384-
385--- The familiar mathematical concept of *permutation* also has an elegant
386--- formulation as an inductive relation. For simplicity, let's focus on
387--- permutations of lists with exactly three elements.
388-
389--- We can define such permutations by the following rules:
390-
391---      ───────────────────────── (perm3_swap12)
392---      Perm3 [a, b, c] [b, a, c]
393-
394---      ───────────────────────── (perm3_swap23)
395---      Perm3 [a, b, c] [a, c, b]
396-
397---   Perm3 l₁ l₂       Perm3 l₂ l₃
398---   ───────────────────────────── (perm3_trans)
399---            Perm3 l₁ l₃
400-
401--- For instance we can derive `Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1]` as follows:
402-
403---   ─────────────────────────(perm3_swap12)   ─────────────────────────(perm3_swap23)
404---   Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [2, 1, 3]                 Perm3 [2, 1, 3] [2, 3, 1]
405---   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────(perm3_trans)   ─────────────────────────(perm3_swap12)
406---   Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [2, 3, 1]                                          Perm3 [2, 3, 1] [3, 2, 1]
407---   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────(perm3_trans)
408---   Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1]
409-
410--- This definition says:
411-
412--- - If `l₂` can be obtained from `l₁` by swapping the first and second
413---   elements, then `l₂` is a permutation of `l₁`.
414-
415--- - If `l₂` can be obtained from `l₁` by swapping the second and third
416---   elements, then `l₂` is a permutation of `l₁`.
417-
418--- - If `l₂` is a permutation of `l₁` and `l₃` is a permutation of `l₂`, then
419---   `l₃` is a permutation of `l₁`.
420-
421--- In Lean, we can define `Perm3` as follows:
422-
423-inductive Perm3 {α : Type} : List α → List α → Prop where
424-  | perm3_swap12 (a b c : α) :
425-      Perm3 [a, b, c] [b, a, c]
426-  | perm3_swap23 (a b c : α) :
427-      Perm3 [a, b, c] [a, c, b]
428-  | perm3_trans (l₁ l₂ l₃ : List α) :
429-      Perm3 l₁ l₂ → Perm3 l₂ l₃ → Perm3 l₁ l₃
430-

435--- ### Example: Evenness (yet again)
436-
437--- We've already seen two ways of stating a proposition that a number `n` is
438--- even: We can say
439-
440--- (1) `even n = true` (using the recursive boolean function `even`), or
441-
442--- (2) `∃ k, n = double k` (using an existential quantifier).
443-
444--- A third possibility, which we'll use as a simple running example in this
445--- chapter, is to say that a number is even if we can *establish* its evenness
446--- from the following two rules:
447-
448---       ———— (ev_0)
449---       Ev 0
450-
451---       Ev n
452---   —————————————— (ev_succ_succ)
453---     Ev (n + 2)
454-
455--- Intuitively these rules say that:
456-
457--- - The number `0` is even.
458--- - If `n` is even, then `n + 2` is even.
459-
460--- (Defining evenness in this way may seem a bit confusing, since we have
461--- already seen two perfectly good ways of doing it. It makes a convenient
462--- running example because it is simple and compact, but we will soon return
463--- to the more compelling examples above.)
464-
465--- To illustrate how this new definition of evenness works, let's imagine
466--- using it to show that `4` is even:
467-
468---           ———— (ev_0)
469---           Ev 0
470---       ———————————— (ev_succ_succ)
471---       Ev (S (S 0))
472---   ———————————————————— (ev_succ_succ)
473---   Ev (S (S (S (S 0))))
474-
475--- In words, to show that `4` is even, by rule `ev_succ_succ`, it suffices to
476--- show that `2` is even. This, in turn, is again guaranteed by rule
477--- `ev_succ_succ`, as long as we can show that `0` is even. But this last fact
478--- follows directly from the `ev_0` rule.
479-
480--- We can translate the informal definition of evenness from above into a
481--- formal `inductive` declaration, where each "way that a number can be even"
482--- corresponds to a separate constructor:
483-
484-inductive Ev : Nat → Prop where
485-  | ev_0                              : Ev 0
486-  | ev_succ_succ (n : Nat) (h : Ev n) : Ev (n + 2)
487-
488--- Such definitions are interestingly different from previous uses of
489--- `inductive` for defining inductive datatypes like `Nat` or `List`. For one
490--- thing, we are defining not a `Type` (like `Nat`) or a function yielding a
491--- `Type` (like `List`), but rather a function from `Nat` to `Prop` -- that
492--- is, a property of numbers. But what is really new is that, because the
493--- `Nat` argument of `Ev` appears to the *right* of the colon on the first
494--- line, it is allowed to take *different* values in the types of different
495--- constructors: `0` in the type of `ev_0` and `(n + 2)` in the type of
496--- `ev_succ_succ`. Accordingly, the type of each constructor must be specified
497--- explicitly (after a colon), and each constructor's type must have the form
498--- `Ev n` for some natural number `n`.
499-
500--- In contrast, recall the definition of `List`:
501-
502-sf_expect_failure
503-  inductive List (α : Type) : Type where
504-    | nil
505-    | cons (x : α) (l : List α)
506-
507--- or (equivalently but more explicitly):
508-
509-sf_expect_failure
510-  inductive List (α : Type) : Type where
511-    | nil                       : List α
512-    | cons (x : α) (l : List α) : List α
513-
514--- This definition introduces the `α` parameter *globally*, to the *left* of
515--- the colon, forcing the result of `nil` and `cons` to be the same type
516--- (i.e., `List α`). But if we had tried to bring `Nat` to the left of the
517--- colon in defining `Ev`, we would have seen an error:
518-
519-sf_expect_failure
520-  inductive WrongEv (n : Nat) : Prop where
521-    | wrong_ev_0 : WrongEv 0
522-    | wrong_ev_succ_succ (h: WrongEv n) : WrongEv (n + 2)
523-
524--- Mismatched inductive type parameter in
525---   WrongEv 0
526--- The provided argument
527---   0
528--- is not definitionally equal to the expected parameter
529---   n
530-
531--- Note: The value of parameter `n` must be fixed throughout the inductive declaration. Consider making this parameter an index if it must vary.
532-
533--- In an `inductive` definition, an argument to the type constructor on the
534--- left of the colon is called a "parameter", whereas an argument on the right
535--- is called an "index" or "annotation."
536-
537--- For example, in `inductive List (α : Type) := ...`, the `α` is a parameter,
538--- while in `inductive Ev : Nat → Prop := ...`, the unnamed `Nat` argument is
539--- an index.
540-
541--- We can think of the inductive definition of `Ev` as defining a Lean
542--- property `Ev : Nat → Prop`, together with two "evidence constructors":
543-
544-#check (Ev.ev_0) -- Ev 0
545-#check Ev.ev_succ_succ -- ∀ (n : Nat) (h : Ev n) : Ev (n + 2)
546-
547--- Indeed, Lean also accepts the following equivalent definition of `Ev`
548-
549-namespace EvPlayground
550-
551-inductive Ev : Nat → Prop where
552-  | ev_0  : Ev 0
553-  | ev_succ_succ : ∀ (n : Nat), Ev n → Ev (n + 2)
554-
555-end EvPlayground
556-
557--- These evidence constructors can be thought of as "primitive evidence of
558--- evenness", and they can be used later on just like proven theorems. In
559--- particular, we can use Lean's `apply` and `exact` tactics with the
560--- constructor names to obtain evidence for `Ev` of particular numbers...
561-
562-theorem ev_4 : Ev 4 := by
563-  apply Ev.ev_succ_succ; apply Ev.ev_succ_succ; exact Ev.ev_0
564-
565--- ... or we can use function application syntax to combine several
566--- constructors:
567-
568-theorem ev_4' : Ev 4 := by
569-  exact Ev.ev_succ_succ 2 (Ev.ev_succ_succ 0 Ev.ev_0)
570-
571--- ... or we can also use the `constructor` tactic we saw earlier to select
572--- the appropriate inductive constructor
573-
574-theorem ev_4'' : Ev 4 := by
575-  constructor; constructor; constructor
576-
577--- In this way, we can also prove theorems that have hypotheses involving
578--- `Ev`.
579-
580-theorem ev_plus4 (n : Nat) (h : Ev n) : Ev (4 + n) := by
581-  rw [Nat.add_comm]
582-  exact (Ev.ev_succ_succ _ (Ev.ev_succ_succ _ h))
583-
584--- ### Exercise (1 star): ev_double ⭐
585-
586-theorem ev_double (n : Nat) : Ev n.double := by
587-  sorry

589--- ### Constructing Evidence for Permutations
590-
591--- Similarly we can apply the evidence constructors to obtain evidence of
592--- `Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1]`:
593-
594-theorem Perm3_rev : Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1] := by
595-  apply Perm3.perm3_trans (l₂:= [2, 3, 1])
596-  . apply Perm3.perm3_trans (l₂:=[2, 1, 3])
597-    . apply Perm3.perm3_swap12
598-    . apply Perm3.perm3_swap23
599-  . apply Perm3.perm3_swap12
600-
601--- And again we can equivalently use function application syntax to combine
602--- several constructors. (Note that the Lean type checker can infer not only
603--- types, but also Nats and List, when they are clear from the context.)
604-
605-theorem Perm3_rev' : Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1] := by
606-  exact (Perm3.perm3_trans _ [2, 3, 1] _
607-          (Perm3.perm3_trans _ [2, 1, 3] _
608-            (Perm3.perm3_swap12 _ _ _)
609-            (Perm3.perm3_swap23 _ _ _))
610-          (Perm3.perm3_swap12 _ _ _))
611-
612--- So the informal derivation trees we drew above are not too far from what's
613--- happening formally. Formally we're using the evidence constructors to build
614--- *evidence trees*, similar to the finite trees we built using the
615--- constructors of data types such as Nat, List, binary trees, etc.
616-
617--- ### Exercise (1 star): Perm3 ⭐
618-
619-theorem Perm3_ex1 : Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [2, 3, 1] := by
620-  sorry
621-
622-theorem Perm3_refl : ∀ (α : Type) (a b c : α ), Perm3 [a, b, c] [a, b, c] := by
623-  sorry
