LF/Preface.lean

1-import LF.SFLCompat
2-
3--- # Preface
4-
5--- ## Welcome
6-
7--- This is the starting point for a series of electronic textbooks on
8--- *Software Foundations*, the mathematical underpinnings of reliable
9--- software. Topics in the series include basic concepts of logic, functional
10--- programming, computer-assisted theorem proving, operational semantics,
11--- logics and techniques for reasoning about programs, static type systems,
12--- property-based random testing, and verification of practical C code. The
13--- exposition is intended for a broad range of readers, from advanced
14--- undergraduates to PhD students and researchers. No specific background in
15--- logic or programming languages is assumed, though a degree of mathematical
16--- maturity will be helpful.
17-
18--- The principal novelty of the series is that it is one hundred percent
19--- formalized and machine-checked: each text is literally a script for Lean.
20--- The books are intended to be read alongside (or inside) an interactive
21--- session with Lean. All the details in the text are fully formalized in
22--- Lean, and almost all of the exercises are designed to be worked using Lean.
23-
24--- This book, *Logical Foundations in Lean*, lays groundwork for the others,
25--- introducing the reader to the basic ideas of functional programming, formal
26--- logic, and Lean itself.
27-
28--- ## Overview
29-
30--- Building reliable software is hard -- really hard. The scale and complexity
31--- of modern systems, the number of people involved, and the range of demands
32--- placed on them make it challenging to build software that is even
33--- more-or-less correct, much less 100% correct. At the same time, the
34--- increasing degree to which information processing is woven into every
35--- aspect of society greatly amplifies the cost of bugs and insecurities.
36-
37--- Computer scientists and software engineers have responded to these
38--- challenges with a host of techniques for improving software reliability,
39--- ranging from recommendations about managing software projects teams (e.g.,
40--- extreme programming) to design philosophies for libraries (e.g.,
41--- model-view-controller, publish-subscribe, etc.) and whole programming
42--- languages (e.g., object-oriented programming, functional programming, ...)
43--- to mathematical techniques for specifying and reasoning about properties of
44--- software and tools for helping validate these properties. The *Software
45--- Foundations* books are focused on this last set of tools.
46-
47--- The present volume weaves together three conceptual threads:
48-
49--- - basic tools from *logic* for making and justifying precise claims about
50---   programs;
51-
52--- - the use of *provers* (or *proof assistants*) to construct rigorous logical
53---   arguments;
54-
55--- - *functional programming*, both as a programming method that simplifies
56---   reasoning about programs and as a bridge between programming and logic.
57-
58--- ### Logic
59-
60--- Logic is the field of study whose subject matter is *proofs* --
61--- unassailable arguments for the truth of particular propositions. Volumes
62--- have been written about the central role of logic in computer science.
63--- called it "the calculus of computer science," while 's paper *On the
64--- Unusual Effectiveness of Logic in Computer Science* catalogs scores of ways
65--- in which logic offers critical tools and insights. Indeed, they observe
66--- that, "As a matter of fact, logic has turned out to be significantly more
67--- effective in computer science than it has been in mathematics. This is
68--- quite remarkable, especially since much of the impetus for the development
69--- of logic during the past one hundred years came from mathematics."
70-
71--- In particular, the fundamental tools of *inductive proof* are ubiquitous
72--- across computer science. You have surely seen them before, perhaps in a
73--- course on discrete math or analysis of algorithms, but in this book we will
74--- examine them more deeply than you have probably done so far.
75-
76--- ### Proof Assistants
77-
78--- The flow of ideas between logic and computer science over the years has run
79--- in both directions, with CS also making contributions to logic. One of
80--- these has been the development of software tools for helping construct and
81--- validate proofs of logical statements. These tools fall into two broad
82--- categories:
83-
84--- - *Automated theorem provers* provide "push-button" operation: you give them
85---   a proposition and they return either *true* or *false* (or, sometimes,
86---   *don't know: ran out of time*). Although their reasoning capabilities are
87---   limited, they have matured tremendously in recent decades and are used now
88---   in a multitude of settings. Examples of such tools include SAT solvers, SMT
89---   solvers, and model checkers.
90-
91--- - *Proof assistants* — or just *provers* — are hybrid tools that automate the
92---   more routine aspects of creating proofs while depending on human guidance
93---   for more difficult aspects. Widely used proof assistants include Isabelle,
94---   Agda, Twelf, ACL2, PVS, F*, HOL4, Rocq, and Lean, among many others.
95-
96--- This course is based around Lean, a proof assistant that has been under
97--- development since 2013 and has attracted a large and active community of
98--- users in both research and at companies like DeepMind, OpenAI, Anthropic,
99--- MSR, and AWS.
100-
101--- Lean provides a rich environment for interactive development of
102--- machine-checked formal reasoning. The kernel of the Lean system is a simple
103--- proof-checker, which guarantees that only correct deduction steps are ever
104--- performed. On top of this kernel, the Lean environment provides high-level
105--- facilities for proof development, including a large library of common
106--- definitions and lemmas, powerful tactics for constructing complex proofs
107--- semi-automatically, and a highly extensible system for defining new
108--- proof-automation tactics and notations for specific situations.
109-
110--- Lean and its relatives have become critical enablers for a [huge variety of
111--- work](https://leanprover-community.github.io/papers.html) across computer
112--- science and mathematics:
113-
114--- - As a *platform for modeling programming languages*, proof assistants have
115---   become standard tools for researchers who need to describe and reason about
116---   complex language definitions. They have been used, for example, to check
117---   the security of the JavaCard platform, obtaining the highest level of
118---   common criteria certification, and for formal specifications of the x86 and
119---   LLVM instruction sets and programming languages such as C.
120-
121--- - As *environments for developing formally certified software and hardware*,
122---   they have been used, for example, to build CompCert, a fully-verified
123---   optimizing compiler for C,
124---   [Cedar](https://github.com/cedar-policy/cedar-spec), a formally-specified
125---   policy language, and CertiKOS, a fully verified hypervisor, for proving the
126---   correctness of subtle algorithms involving floating point numbers, and as
127---   the basis for CertiCrypt, FCF, and SSProve, which are frameworks for
128---   proving cryptographic algorithms secure. They are also being used to build
129---   verified implementations of the open-source RISC-V processor architecture.
130-
131--- - As *proof assistants for mathematics*, they have been used to validate and
132---   help develop a number of important results. For example, the ability to
133---   include complex computations inside proofs made it possible to develop the
134---   first formally verified proof of the 4-color theorem. This proof had
135---   previously been controversial among mathematicians because it required
136---   checking a large number of configurations using a program. More recently,
137---   an even more massive effort led to a formalization of the Feit-Thompson
138---   Theorem, the first major step in the classification of finite simple
139---   groups. Specifically, Lean is currently at the core of various
140---   formalization efforts in mathematics, such as the proof of [Fermat's Last
141---   Theorem](https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/FLT), the [Sphere Packing
142---   Problem](https://github.com/thefundamentaltheor3m/Sphere-Packing-Lean). and
143---   even DeepMind's AI model for IMO problems
144---   [AlphaProof](https://deepmind.google/blog/ai-solves-imo-problems-at-silver-medal-level/).
145-
146--- ### Functional Programming
147-
148--- *Functional programming* refers both to a collection of idioms that can be
149--- used in almost any programming language and to a family of languages
150--- designed to foreground these idioms, including Haskell, OCaml, Standard ML,
151--- F#, Scala, Scheme, Racket, Common Lisp, Clojure, Erlang, F*, and Lean
152--- itself.
153-
154--- Functional programming has been developed over many decades — indeed, its
155--- roots go back to Church's lambda-calculus from the 1930s, well *before* the
156--- first electronic computers! But since the early '90s it has enjoyed a surge
157--- of interest among both software engineers and language designers.
158-
159--- The most basic tenet of functional programming is that, whenever possible,
160--- computation should be *pure*, in the sense that the only effect of
161--- execution should be to produce a result: it should be free from *side
162--- effects* such as I/O, assignments to mutable variables, redirecting
163--- pointers, etc. For example, whereas an *imperative* sorting function might
164--- take a list of numbers and rearrange its pointers to put the list in order,
165--- a pure sorting function would take the original list and return a fresh
166--- list containing the same numbers in sorted order.
167-
168--- A significant benefit of this style of programming is that it makes
169--- programs easier to understand and reason about. If every operation on a
170--- data structure yields a new data structure, leaving the old one intact,
171--- then there is no need to worry about how that structure is being shared and
172--- whether a change by one part of the program might break an invariant relied
173--- on by another part of the program. These considerations are particularly
174--- critical in concurrent systems, where every piece of mutable state shared
175--- between threads is a potential source of pernicious bugs.
176-
177--- Another reason for the popularity of functional programming is related to
178--- the first: functional programs are often much easier to parallelize and
179--- physically distribute than their imperative counterparts. If running a
180--- computation has no effect other than producing a result, then it does not
181--- matter *where* it is run. Similarly, if a data structure is never modified
182--- destructively, it can be copied freely, across cores or across the network.
183--- Indeed, the "Map-Reduce" idiom, which lies at the heart of massively
184--- distributed query processors like Hadoop and is used by Google to index the
185--- entire web, is a classic example of functional programming.
186-
187--- For purposes of these books, functional programming has yet another
188--- significant attraction: it serves as a bridge between logic and computer
189--- science. Indeed, Lean itself can be viewed as a combination of a small but
190--- extremely expressive functional programming language and a set of tools for
191--- stating and proving logical assertions. Moreover, when we come to look more
192--- closely, we find that these two sides of Lean are actually aspects of the
193--- very same underlying machinery -- i.e., *proofs are programs*.
194-
195--- ### Further Reading
196-
197--- This text is intended to be self contained, but readers looking for
198--- follow-on textbooks or deeper treatments of particular topics will find
199--- some suggestions for further reading in the Postscript chapter.
200-
201--- ## Practicalities
202-
203--- ### System Requirements
204-
205--- Lean runs on Windows, Linux, and MacOS. The files in this book have been
206--- tested with Lean version `4.33.0`.
207-
208--- ### Installation
209-
210--- The Visual Studio Code IDE is the recommended platform for using Lean.
211-
212--- - Install VS Code if needed
213-
214--- - From the Extensions tab of VS Code, install the Lean 4 extension
215-
216--- - Clone the [SF-in-Lean](https://github.com/plclub/sf-in-lean) git repo and
217---   open it in VS Code
218-
219--- - The first time you open a Lean file, the extension will offer to install
220---   Lean itself; accept, and it will fetch the version this book needs
221-
222--- - Wait for Lean to build the project (it takes a few minutes)
223-
224--- ### Exercises
225-
226--- Each chapter includes numerous exercises. Each is marked with a "star
227--- rating," which can be interpreted as follows:
228-
229--- - One star: easy exercises that underscore points in the text and that, for
230---   most readers, should take only a minute or two. Get in the habit of working
231---   these as you reach them.
232-
233--- - Two stars: straightforward exercises (five or ten minutes).
234-
235--- - Three stars: exercises requiring a bit of thought (ten minutes to half an
236---   hour).
237-
238--- - Four and five stars: more difficult exercises (half an hour and up).
239-
240--- Those using SF in a classroom setting should note that the autograder
241--- assigns extra points to harder exercises:
242-
243--- 1 star  = 1 point
244--- 2 stars = 2 points
245--- 3 stars = 3 points
246--- 4 stars = 6 points
247--- 5 stars = 10 points
248-
249--- Some exercises are marked "advanced," and some are marked "optional." Doing
250--- just the non-optional, non-advanced exercises should provide good coverage
251--- of the core material. Optional exercises provide a bit of extra practice
252--- with key concepts and introduce secondary themes that may be of interest to
253--- some readers. Advanced exercises offer an extra challenge and a deeper cut
254--- at the ideas.
255-
256--- ### Citation Format
257-
258--- If you want to refer to this volume in your own writing, please do so as
259--- follows:
260-
261--- @book            {SFL:1,
262--- author       =   {Mike Hicks and Benjamin C. Pierce and the SF-in-Lean team},
263--- title        =   "Logical Foundations",
264--- series       =   "Software Foundations in Lean",
265--- volume       =   "1",
266--- year         =   "2026",
267--- publisher    =   "Electronic textbook",
268--- note         =   {Version 0.1.0, \URL<https://github.com/plclub/sf-in-lean>}
269--- }
270-
271--- ## For Potential Contributors
272-
273--- If you find things you'd like to help add or improve, your contributions
274--- are welcome! To get started, clone the [SF-in-Lean git
275--- repo](https://github.com/plclub/sf-in-lean) and have a look at
276--- `ALPHATESTERS.md`.
277-
278--- ## For Instructors
279-
280--- A large compendium of exams from many offerings of CIS5000 ("Software
281--- Foundations") at the University of Pennsylvania can be found at
282--- <https://www.seas.upenn.edu/~cis5000/current/exams/index.html>. Until 2026,
283--- the course was offered in Rocq, but the ideas behind the problems are still
284--- relevant.
285-

1-module
2-
3-public meta import Lean.Elab.BuiltinCommand
4-
5-namespace SLFCommand
6-
7-open Lean Elab Command
8-
9-meta section
10-
11--- Copied from `SubVerso.Compat` to avoid making generated projects depend on verso.
12--- We want to have info state and messages available right after the elaboration,
13--- so we need to disable `Elab.async` which would let diagnostics produced asynchronously
14--- through spanshot tasks.
15-private def commandWithoutAsync (act : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
16-  match (← get).scopes with
17-  | [] => act
18-  | h :: t =>
19-    let mut orig : Option Bool := none
20-    try
21-      orig := h.opts.get? `Elab.async
22-      modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := h.opts.setBool `Elab.async false } :: t }
23-      act
24-    finally
25-      if let h :: t := (← get).scopes then
26-        let opts := orig.map (h.opts.setBool `Elab.async) |>.getD (h.opts.erase `Elab.async)
27-        modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := opts } :: t }
28-
29-private def withRestoringState (keepMsgs : Bool) (m : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
30-  let savedState ← get
31-  try
32-    m
33-  finally
34-    let state ← get
35-    set { savedState with
36-      -- Preserve the info tree
37-      infoState := state.infoState
38-      messages := if keepMsgs then state.messages else savedState.messages }
39-
40-namespace IndentedCommands
41-
42-/-! # Block Commands Parser
43-  Parse an indented command block. Commands are separated by new lines.
44-  Since we want to capture parsing errors in `sf_expect_failure`,
45-  we can't use Lean command parser directly in our command's syntax,
46-  because any parsing error occurred would fail `sf_expect_failure` itself.
47-  One possible solution is to first parse the whole indented body as raw syntax,
48-  and then run Lean's command parser followed by command elaboration.
49--/
50-
51-open Parser
52-
53-private def rawLineEndFn : ParserFn :=
54-  eoiFn <|> satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break"
55-
56-/-- Consumes everything until the next newline and then consumes the newline itself. -/
57-private def rawLineFn : ParserFn :=
58-  takeUntilFn (· == '\n') >> rawLineEndFn
59-
60-/- For each line after the first body line, consumes leading whitespaces.
61-  If it's blank, consumes the newline; otherwise consumes the line
62-  requiring the indentation.
63--/
64-private def rawIndentedLineFn : ParserFn := atomicFn <|
65-  takeWhileFn (· == ' ') >>
66-  (satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break" <|>
67-    (checkColGeFn "indented command sequence" >> rawLineFn))
68-
69-private def rawCommandBlockFn : ParserFn :=
70-  rawFn (rawLineFn >> manyFn rawIndentedLineFn) (trailingWs := true)
71-
72-private def rawCommandBlock : Parser := { fn := rawCommandBlockFn }
73-
74-@[combinator_parenthesizer rawCommandBlock]
75-private def rawCommandBlock.parenthesizer := PrettyPrinter.Parenthesizer.visitToken
76-
77-@[combinator_formatter rawCommandBlock]
78-private def rawCommandBlock.formatter := PrettyPrinter.Formatter.visitAtom Name.anonymous
79-
80-private partial def runRawCmdsAux
81-    (ictx : InputContext) (pstate : ModuleParserState) : CommandElabM Unit := do
82-  let state ← get
83-  let scope := state.scopes.head!
84-  let pctx :=  {
85-      env := state.env
86-      options := scope.opts
87-      currNamespace := scope.currNamespace
88-      openDecls := scope.openDecls : ParserModuleContext
89-    }
90-  let (cmd, pstate, messages) := parseCommand ictx pctx pstate state.messages
91-  modify fun state => { state with messages }
92-  unless cmd.isOfKind ``Command.eoi do
93-    elabCommand cmd
94-    runLinters cmd
95-    unless isTerminalCommand cmd do
96-      runRawCmdsAux ictx pstate
97-
98-/- Recovers the source info and elaborates the commands -/
99-private def runRawCmds (body : Syntax) : CommandElabM Unit := do
100-  let some source := body.getSubstring? (withLeading := false) (withTrailing := false)
101-    | throwErrorAt body "command sequence has no source range"
102-  let fileName ← getFileName
103-  let fileMap ← getFileMap
104-  -- Recall that `rawIndentedLineFn` may consume whitespaces after the newline.
105-  -- Here we move the ending back to the last non-whitespace character to produce
106-  -- correctly positioned diagnostics.
107-  let stopPos := source.trimRight.stopPos
108-  if h : stopPos ≤ fileMap.source.rawEndPos then
109-    let ictx := InputContext.mk fileMap.source fileName
110-      (fileMap := fileMap) (endPos := stopPos) (endPos_valid := h)
111-    runRawCmdsAux ictx { pos := source.startPos, recovering := false, hasLeading := false }
112-  else
113-    throwErrorAt body "invalid command-sequence source range"
114-
115-end IndentedCommands
116-
117-end
118-
119-public meta section
120-
121-open Parser IndentedCommands
122-
123-/--
124-Elaborates the enclosed commands and reports their diagnostics,
125-but discards their effects afterwards.
126-
127-Example:
128-```lean
129-sf_experiment
130-  def hidden : Nat := 1
131-  #check hidden
132--- `hidden` is not available here.
133-```
134--/
135-def experimentTk := leading_parser
136-  "sf_experiment"
137-
138-@[command_parser] def experimentCmd := leading_parser
139-  experimentTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
140-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
141-
142-/--
143-Succeeds only if the enclosed commands fail.
144-Diagnostics from the expected failure are suppressed.
145-
146-Example:
147-```lean
148-sf_expect_failure
149-  example : 1 = 2 := rfl
150-```
151--/
152-def expectFailureTk := leading_parser
153-  "sf_expect_failure"
154-
155-/-
156-  Like `sf_expect_failure` but reports the diagnostics.
157--/
158-def expectFailureInfoTk := leading_parser
159-  "sf_expect_failure?"
160-
161-@[command_parser] def expectFailureCmd := leading_parser
162-  expectFailureTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
163-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
164-
165-@[command_parser] def expectFailureInfoCmd := leading_parser
166-  expectFailureInfoTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
167-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
168-
169-@[command_elab experimentCmd]
170-def elabExperimentCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
171-  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
172-  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState true do
173-    runRawCmds body
174-
175-@[command_elab expectFailureCmd, command_elab expectFailureInfoCmd]
176-def elabExpectFailureCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
177-  let keepMsgs := stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureInfoCmd
178-  unless keepMsgs || stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureCmd do
179-    throwUnsupportedSyntax
180-  let tk := stx[0]
181-  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
182-  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState keepMsgs do
183-    withRef tk <| failIfSucceeds <| runRawCmds body
184-
185-end
186-
187-namespace Tests

LF/Tactics.lean

1-import LF.Poly
2-import LF.CustomTactics
3-
4-import LF.SFLCompat
5-
6--- # Tactics: More Basic Tactics
7-
8--- This chapter introduces several additional proof strategies and tactics
9--- that allow us to begin proving more interesting properties of functional
10--- programs.
11-
12--- We will see:
13-
14--- - how to use auxiliary lemmas in both "forward-" and "backward-style" proofs;
15-
16--- - how to reason about data constructors -- in particular, how to use the fact
17---   that they are injective and disjoint;
18-
19--- - how to strengthen an induction hypothesis, and when such strengthening is
20---   required; and
21-
22--- - more details on how to reason by case analysis.
23-
24--- OA: added these to use Lean's Nat.
25-
26-open Nat (add_comm add_assoc add_zero add_succ mul_one succ_sub_succ)
27-
28--- ## The `apply` Tactic
29-
30--- We often encounter situations where the goal to be proved is *exactly* the
31--- same as some hypothesis in the context or some previously proved lemma.
32-
33-theorem silly1 (n m : Nat) : n = m → n = m := by
34-  intro eq
35-  /- Here, we could finish with `rw [eq]` as we
36-    have done several times before.  Or we can finish
37-    by using `apply`: -/
38-  apply eq
39-
40--- The `apply` tactic also works with *conditional* hypotheses and lemmas: if
41--- the statement being applied is an implication, then the premises of this
42--- implication will be added to the list of subgoals needing to be proved.
43-
44-theorem silly2 (n m o p : Nat) :
45-    n = m →
46-    (n = m → [n, o] = [m, p]) →
47-    [n, o] = [m, p] := by
48-  intro eq1 eq2
49-  apply eq2
50-  apply eq1
51-
52--- Typically, when we use `apply h`, the statement `h` will begin with a
53--- `forall` that introduces some *universally quantified variables*.
54-
55--- When Lean matches the current goal against the conclusion of `h`, it will
56--- try to find appropriate values for these variables. For example, when we do
57--- `apply eq2` in the following proof, the universal variable `q` in `eq2`
58--- gets instantiated with `n`, and `r` gets instantiated with `m`.
59-
60-theorem silly2a (n m : Nat) :
61-    (n, n) = (m, m)  →
62-    (∀ (q r : Nat), (q, q) = (r, r) → [q] = [r]) →
63-    [n] = [m] := by
64-  intro eq1 eq2
65-  apply eq2
66-  apply eq1
67-
68--- ### Exercise (2 stars): silly_ex ⭐⭐
69-
70--- Complete the following proof using only `intros` and `apply`.
71-
72-theorem silly_ex p :
73-    (∀ (n : Nat), n.even = true → (n + 1).even = false) →
74-    (∀ (n : Nat), n.even = false → n.odd = true) →
75-    p.even = true →
76-    (p + 1).odd = true := by
77-  sorry
78-
79--- To use the `apply` tactic, the (conclusion of the) fact being applied must
80--- match the goal exactly (perhaps after simplification) -- for example,
81--- `apply` will not work if the left and right sides of the equality are
82--- swapped.
83-
84-theorem silly3 (n m : Nat) :
85-    n = m →
86-    m = n := by
87-  intro H
88-  -- Here we cannot use `apply` directly...
89-  /- ...but we can use the `symm` tactic, which switches the left
90-      and right sides of an equality in the goal. -/
91-  symm; apply H
92-
93--- ### Exercise (2 stars): apply_exercise1 ⭐⭐
94-
95--- You can use `apply` with previously defined theorems, not just hypotheses
96--- in the context. Use a previously-defined theorem about `rev` from Poly. Use
97--- that theorem as part of your (relatively short) solution to this exercise.
98--- You do not need `induction`.
99-
100-theorem rev_exercise1 {α} (l l' : List α) :
101-    l = l'.rev →
102-    l' = l.rev := by
103-  intro eq
104-  rw [eq]; symm
105-  apply reverse_reverse
106-  -- /ADMITTED
107-
108--- ### Exercise (1 star): apply_rewrite (manually graded) ⭐
109-
110--- Briefly explain the difference between the tactics `apply` and `rw`. What
111--- are the situations where both can usefully be applied?
112-
113--- ### Supplying arguments to `apply`
114-
115--- The following silly example uses two rewrites in a row to get from `\[a;b`]
116--- to `\[e;f`].
117-
118-theorem trans_eq_example (a b c d e f : Nat) :
119-    [a, b] = [c, d] →
120-    [c, d] = [e, f] →
121-    [a, b] = [e, f] := by
122-  intro eq1 eq2
123-  rw [eq1, eq2]
124-
125--- Since this is a common pattern, we might like to pull it out as a lemma
126--- that records, once and for all, the fact that equality is transitive.
127-
128-theorem trans_eq {α : Type} (x y z : α) :
129-    x = y → y = z → x = z := by
130-  intro eq1 eq2
131-  rw [eq1, eq2]
132-
133--- Nowwe **should** be able to use `trans_eq` to prove the above example.
134-
135--- But it doesn't *quite* work. If we simply tell Lean `apply
136--- trans_eq` after
137--- the `intro`, it can tell (by matching the goal against the conclusion of
138--- the lemma) that it should instantiate `α` with `List Nat`, `x` with
139--- `[a, b]`, and `z` with `[e,f]`. However, the matching process doesn't
140--- determine an instantiation for `y`, nor does it know which hypothese to use
141--- for the premises to `trans_eq`.
142-
143-theorem trans_eq_example' (a b c d e f : Nat) :
144-    [a, b] = [c, d] →
145-    [c, d] = [e, f] →
146-    [a, b] = [e, f] := by
147-  intro eq1 eq2
148-  apply trans_eq
149-  sorry
150-  sorry
151-  sorry
152-
153--- As we saw earlier, `apply` would generate new goals for these premises, and
154--- we could finish the proof by explicitly applying these hypotheses to those
155--- new goals. But we can also be more direct by supplying those hypotheses
156--- directly to `apply`.
157-
158-theorem trans_eq_example'' (a b c d e f : Nat) :
159-    [a, b] = [c, d] →
160-    [c, d] = [e, f] →
161-    [a, b] = [e, f] := by
162-  intro eq1 eq2
163-  apply trans_eq [a, b] [c, d] [e, f] eq1 eq2
164-
165--- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1, NOW):
166---     This and below are new (my addition), thoughts?
167-
168--- In the previous example, we had to specify the `x` and `z` arguments to
169--- `trans_eq` before we could supply `[c, d]` for `y` or `eq1` and `eq2` for
170--- the premises. However, we just said that Lean was able to infer these
171--- arguments, so it's a bit redundant (and wordy) for us to do it. Thankfully,
172--- Lean allows us to use `_`s for positional arguments that it can infer.
173-
174-theorem trans_eq_example''' (a b c d e f : Nat) :
175-    [a, b] = [c, d] →
176-    [c, d] = [e, f] →
177-    [a, b] = [e, f] := by
178-  intro eq1 eq2
179-  apply trans_eq _ _ _ eq1 eq2
180-
181--- Aside: if we know the name of the argument we are supplying (in this case
182--- `y`), we can just name it directly and avoid typing any `_`s.
183-
184-theorem trans_eq_example'''' (a b c d e f : Nat) :
185-    [a, b] = [c, d] →
186-    [c, d] = [e, f] →
187-    [a, b] = [e, f] := by
188-  intro eq1 eq2
189-  apply trans_eq (y := [c, d])
190-  apply eq1
191-  apply eq2
192-
193--- Like any other kind of software, there are conventions and best practices
194--- associated with writing proofs in Lean. One of these conventions concerns
195--- the use of the `exact` tactic. When fully applying another theorem like in
196--- the previous examples, it is considered good practice to use the `exact`
197--- tactic instead of `apply`. This signals to a reader of the proof that the
198--- proof is "exactly" an instance of another lemma, and that nothing of
199--- particular interest is happening here. This achieves a similar goal as when
200--- a mathematician says that one result is "just" an instance of another.
201-
202-theorem trans_eq_example_exact (a b c d e f : Nat) :
203-    [a, b] = [c, d] →
204-    [c, d] = [e, f] →
205-    [a, b] = [e, f] := by
206-  intro eq1 eq2
207-  exact trans_eq _ _ _ eq1 eq2
208-

210---     if we decide we want to introduce `calc` earlier, we can remove this
211---     explanation or tweak it. BCP: I think we did introduce it earlier...

214--- as applying `trans_eq`. The tactic allows us to specify the in-between
215--- states of any transitive relation. The notation is reminiscent of the
216--- proofs you might see in a mathematics textbook.

235--- ## The `injection` and `contradiction` Tactics
236-
237--- Recall the definition of natural numbers:
238-
239---   inductive Nat : Type :=
240---     | zero
241---     | succ (n : Nat).
242-
243--- It is obvious from this definition that every number has one of two forms:
244--- either it is the constructor `0` or it is built by applying the constructor
245--- `.succ` to another number. But there is more here than meets the eye:
246--- implicit in the definition are two additional facts:
247-
248--- - The constructor `.succ` is *injective* (or *one-to-one*). That is, if
249---   `n + 1 = m + 1`, it must also be that `n = m`.
250-
251--- - The constructors `0` and `.succ` are *disjoint*. That is, `0` is not equal
252---   to `n + 1` for any `n`.
253-
254--- Similar principles apply to every inductively defined type: all
255--- constructors are injective, and the values built from distinct constructors
256--- are never equal. For lists, the `cons` constructor is injective and the
257--- empty list `nil` is different from every non-empty list. For booleans,
258--- `true` and `false` are different. (Since `true` and `false` take no
259--- arguments, their injectivity is neither here nor there.) And so on.
260-
261--- SOON: FSR'25 - I wrote an explanation for `have` here, though I feel its
262--- inclusion here breaks the flow.
263-
264--- Lean's `have` tactic, used above, adds the given hypothesis to the context,
265--- but it first requires you to prove the hypothesis as a new goal.
266-
267--- This technique for injectivity can be generalized to any constructor by
268--- writing the equivalent of `pred` -- i.e., writing a function that "undoes"
269--- one application of the constructor.
270-
271--- As a convenient alternative, Lean provides a tactic called `injection` that
272--- allows us to exploit the injectivity of any constructor. Here is an
273--- alternate proof of the above theorem using `injection`:
274-
275-theorem succ_injective' (n m : Nat) :
276-    n + 1 = m + 1 →
277-    n = m := by
278-  intro h
279-  injection h with hmn
280-
281--- By writing `injection h with hmn` at this point, we are asking Lean to
282--- generate all equations that it can infer from `h` using the injectivity of
283--- constructors (in the present example, the equation `n = m`). This equation
284--- is added as a hypothesis (called `hmn` in this case) into the context.
285--- Because this equation is exactly our goal, in this case the `injection`
286--- tactic is able to automatically close the goal.
287-
288--- Here's a more interesting example that shows how `injection` can derive
289--- multiple equations at once.
290-
291-theorem injection_ex1 (n m o : Nat) :
292-    [n, m] = [o, o] →
293-    n = m := by
294-  intro h
295-  all_goals
296-    injection h with h1 h2
297-    injection h2 with h3
298-    rw [h1, h3]
299-
300--- There is also a related tactic, `injections`, that applies the `injection`
301--- tactic to all your hypotheses at once, as many times in a row as it can.
302--- Using this tactic can avoid needing to repeatedly use `injection` on lists,
303--- for example.
304-
305-theorem injection_ex2 (n m o : Nat) :
306-    [n, m] = [o, o] →
307-    n = m := by
308-  intro h
309-  all_goals
310-    injections h1 _ h3
311-    rw [h1, h3]
312-
313--- ### Exercise (3 stars): injection_ex3 ⭐⭐⭐
314-
315-theorem injection_ex3 {α : Type} (x y z : α) (l j : List α) :
316-    x :: y :: l = z :: j →
317-    j = z :: l →
318-    x = y := by
319-  intro eq1 eq2
320-  injections hxz hyl_j
321-  have hyl_zl : y :: l = z :: l := by rw [hyl_j, eq2]
322-  injections hyz
323-  rw [hxz, hyz]
324-
325--- So much for injectivity of constructors. What about disjointness?
326-
327--- The principle of disjointness says that two terms beginning with different
328--- constructors (like `0` and `succ`, or `true` and `false`) can never be
329--- equal. This means that, any time we find ourselves in a context where we've
330--- *assumed* that two such terms are equal, we are justified in concluding
331--- anything we want, since the assumption is nonsensical.
332-
333--- The `contradiction` tactic, which we've already seen for handling cases
334--- where we have assumed `False`, also embodies this principle: if we have a a
335--- hypothesis involving an equality between different constructors (e.g.,
336--- `false = true`), `contradiction` solves the current goal immediately. Some
337--- examples:
338-
339-theorem disjoint_ex1 (n m : Nat) :
340-    false = true →
341-    n = m := by
342-  intro contra
343-  contradiction
344-
345-theorem disjoint_ex2 (n : Nat) :
346-    n + 1 = 0 →
347-    2 + 2 = 5 := by
348-  intro contra
349-  contradiction
350-
351--- These examples are instances of a logical principle known as the *principle
352--- of explosion*, which asserts that a contradictory hypothesis entails
353--- anything (even manifestly false things!).
354-
355--- If you find the principle of explosion confusing, remember that these
356--- proofs are *not* simply showing that the conclusion of the statement holds.
357--- Rather, they are showing that, *if* the nonsensical situation described by
358--- the premise did somehow hold, *then* the nonsensical conclusion would hold
359--- too (because we'd be living in an inconsistent universe where every
360--- statement is true).
361-
362--- We'll explore the principle of explosion in more detail in the next
363--- chapter.
364-
365--- ### Exercise (1 star): disjoint_ex3 ⭐
366-
367-theorem disjoint_ex3 {α : Type} (x y z : α) (l : List α) :
368-    x :: y :: l = [] →
369-    x = z := by
370-  sorry
371-
372--- For a more useful example, we can use `contradiction` to make a connection
373--- between the two different notions of equality (`=` and `==`) that we have
374--- seen for natural numbers.
375-
376-theorem beq_0_l (n : Nat) :
377-    (0 == n) = true →
378-    n = 0 := by
379-  intro h
380-  -- We can proceed by case analysis on `n`. The first case is trivial.
381-  cases n
382-  case zero => rfl
383-    -- However, the second one doesn't look so simple: assuming
384-    -- `(0 == n' + 1) = true`, we must show `n' + 1 = 0`!  The way forward
385-    -- is to observe that the assumption itself is nonsensical:
386-  case succ n' =>
387-    -- If we use `contradiction` here, Lean confirms that the subgoal
388-    -- we are working on is impossible and removes it from further
389-    -- consideration.
390-    contradiction

477--- The injectivity of constructors allows us to reason that
478--- `∀ (n m : Nat), n + 1 = m + 1 → n = m`. The converse of this implication is
479--- an instance of a more general fact about both constructors and functions,
480--- which we will find useful below:
481-
482-theorem function_congruence {α β : Type} (f : α → β) (x y : α) :
483-    x = y → f x = f y := by
484-  intro eq
485-  rw [eq]

487-theorem eq_implies_succ_equal (n m : Nat) :
488-    n = m → n + 1 = m + 1 := by
489-  intro eq
490-  rw [eq]
491-
492--- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1, NOW):
493---     can someone double check me on this? I think `congr` works this way but
494---     I want to be sure
495-
496--- Indeed, there is also a tactic named `congr` that can prove such theorems
497--- directly. Given a goal of the form `f a1 ... an = g b1 ... bn`, the tactic
498--- `congr` will produce subgoals of the form `f = g`, `a1 = b1`, ...,
499--- `an = bn`. At the same time, any of these subgoals that are simple enough
500--- (e.g., immediately provable by `rfl`) will be automatically discharged.
501-
502-theorem eq_implies_succ_equal' (n m : Nat) :
503-    n = m → n + 1 = m + 1 := by
504-  intro eq
505-  congr
506-
507--- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1, NOW):
508---     how is this explanation of `congr`?
509-
510--- The `congr` tactic also accepts a numerical argument, which tells Lean how
511--- deeply to decompose the goal. So, given a goal like
512--- `((a, b), (c, d)) = ((e, f), (g, h))`, `congr 1` only applies `congr` once
513--- to the goal, and would produce two subgoals: `(a, b) = (e, f)` and
514--- `(c, d) = (g, h)`. `congr 2`, meanwhile, would apply `congr` again to both
515--- these subgoals, and produce four subgoals: `a = e`, `b = f`, `c = g` and
516--- `d = h`. Using `congr` without an argument always decomposes the goal as
517--- deeply as possible.
518-
519--- Why does Lean provide this level of flexibility? Depending on what we are
520--- trying to prove, deeper applications of `congr` may make our goal
521--- unprovable. Consider this example:
522-
523-example (a b c d : Nat) :
524-    a = b → c = d → (a, c + 1) = (b, 1 + d) := by
525-  intro eq1 eq2
526-  congr
527-  /- We now have three goals: `c = 1`, `1 = d`, and `1 = d`,
528-     but these are not provable from our hypotheses! `congr`
529-     has gone too deep. -/
530-  sorry
531-  sorry
532-  sorry

534-theorem eq_implies_succ_proj_equal (a b c d : Nat) :
535-    a = b → c = d → (a, c + 1) = (b, 1 + d) := by
536-  intro eq1 eq2
537-  /- Only shallowly using `congr` here allows us to complete the proof -/
538-  congr 1
539-  rw [add_comm]
540-  congr

542--- ## Using Tactics on Hypotheses
543-
544--- By default, most tactics work on the goal formula and leave the context
545--- unchanged. However, most tactics also have a variant that performs a
546--- similar operation on a statement in the context.
547-
548--- For example, the tactic "`dsimp at H`" performs simplification on the
549--- hypothesis `H` in the context.
550-
551-theorem beq_succ (n m : Nat) : (n + 1 == m + 1) = (n == m) :=
552-  decide_eq_decide.mpr Nat.succ_inj
553-
554-theorem succ_inj (n m : Nat) :
555-    n + 1 == m + 1 → n == m := by
556-  intro h
557-  rw [beq_succ] at h
558-  exact h
559-
560--- Similarly, `apply L at H` matches some conditional statement `L` (of the
561--- form `X → Y`, say) against a hypothesis `H` in the context. However, unlike
562--- ordinary `apply` (which rewrites a goal matching `Y` into a subgoal `X`),
563--- `apply L at H` matches `H` against `X` and, if successful, replaces it with
564--- `Y`.
565-
566--- In other words, `apply L at H` gives us a form of "forward reasoning":
567--- given `X → Y` and a hypothesis matching `X`, it produces a hypothesis
568--- matching `Y`.
569-
570--- By contrast, `apply L` is "backward reasoning": it says that if we know
571--- `X → Y` and we are trying to prove `Y`, it suffices to prove `X`.
572-
573--- Here is a variant of a proof that uses forward reasoning throughout instead
574--- of backward reasoning.
575-
576-theorem silly4 (n m p q : Nat) :
577-    (n = m → p = q) →
578-    n = m →
579-    p = q := by
580-  intro eq1 eq2
581-  apply eq1 at eq2
582-  exact eq2
583-
584--- Forward reasoning starts from what is *given* (premises, previously proven
585--- theorems) and iteratively draws conclusions from them until the goal is
586--- reached. Backward reasoning starts from the *goal* and iteratively reasons
587--- about what would imply the goal, until premises or previously proven
588--- theorems are reached.
589-
590--- The informal proofs seen in math or computer science classes tend to use
591--- forward reasoning. By contrast, idiomatic use of Lean generally favors
592--- backward reasoning, though in some situations the forward style can be
593--- easier to think about.
594-
595--- You may be interested to know that the `apply ... at ...` tactic is not
596--- part of Lean's base set of tactics. However, Lean makes it very easy for
597--- users to define new tactics that suit their particular proof style, and so
598--- the developers of the popular Mathlib library defined the
599--- `apply ... at ...` tactic to better enable forward reasoning. Mathlib is a
600--- very large development, so we won't import the whole thing here, but we
601--- have provided you `apply ... at ...` because it is quite useful.
602-
603--- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1, NOW):
604---     this part has been changed from the original Rocq, let me know what you
605---     think
606-
607--- ## Specializing Hypotheses
608-
609--- We've already seen how we can use `have` to do forward reasoning, by
610--- letting us state and prove useful facts that get us closer to the main goal
611--- we're trying to prove. Often, though, these facts are just special cases of
612--- more general hypotheses we already have.
613-
614--- If `h` is a quantified hypothesis in the current context -- i.e.,
615--- `h : forall (x : α), P` -- then `have h := h (x := e)` will change `h` so
616--- that it looks like `P` with `x` replaced by `e`.
617-
618--- For example:
619-
620-theorem have_example m :
621-    (∀ n, m * n = 0) → m = 0 := by
622-  intro h
623-  have h := h (n := 1)
624-  rw [mul_one] at h
625-  exact h
626-
627--- You may notice that, in the above proof, after using `have` we were left
628--- with a leftover hypothesis in the context, the old `h`, so to speak. Often
629--- we don't care to keep this old hypothesis around, and so we can use the
630--- `replace` tactic instead. It behaves the same as `have`, except it gets rid
631--- of the old hypothesis afterwards:
632-
633-theorem replace_example m :
634-    (∀ n, m * n = 0) → m = 0 := by
635-  intro h
636-  replace h := h (n := 1)
637-  rw [mul_one] at h
638-  exact h
639-
640--- ### Exercise (3 stars): nth_error_always_none ⭐⭐⭐
641-
642--- Use `have` or `replace` to prove the the following lemma, following the
643--- model of the examples above. Do not use `induction`.
644-
645-theorem nth?_always_none (l : List Nat) :
646-    (∀ i, nth? l i = none) →
647-    l = [] := by
648-  sorry
649-
650--- Tactics like `have` and `replace` can also be used with lemmas and theorems
651--- we've already proven, not just things in our context. Using these tactis
652--- before `apply` gives us yet another way to control where `apply` does its
653--- work.
654-
655-theorem trans_eq_example'''''' (a b c d e f : Nat) :
656-    [a, b] = [c, d] →
657-    [c, d] = [e, f] →
658-    [a, b] = [e, f] := by
659-  intros eq1 eq2
660-  have h := trans_eq (y:= [c, d])
661-  apply h
662-  /- This tactic closes a goal if it appears anywhere in the context.
663-     In this case we could also write `exact eq1` ... -/
664-  assumption
665-  /- .. and here we could also write `exact eq2` -/
666-  assumption

668--- ## Varying the Induction Hypothesis
669-
670--- Sometimes it is important to control the exact form of the induction
671--- hypothesis when carrying out inductive proofs in Lean. In particular, we
672--- may need to be careful about which of the assumptions we move (using
673--- `intro`) from the goal to the context before invoking the `induction`
674--- tactic.
675-
676--- For example, suppose we want to show that `double` is injective -- i.e.,
677--- that it maps different arguments to different results:
678-
679---   theorem double_injective: forall n m,
680---     double n = double m →
681---     n = m
682-
683--- The way we start this proof is a bit delicate: if we begin it with
684-
685---   intro n; induction n
686-
687--- then all will be well. But if we begin it with introducing *both* variables
688-
689---   intros n m; induction n
690-
691--- we get stuck in the middle of the inductive case...
692-
693-example (n m : Nat) :
694-    n.double = m.double →
695-    n = m := by
696-  induction n
697-  case zero =>
698-    rw [Nat.double_zero]
699-    intro eq
700-    cases m
701-    case zero => rfl
702-    case succ _ => rw [Nat.double_succ] at eq; contradiction
703-  case succ n' ih =>
704-    intro eq
705-    cases m
706-    case zero => rw [Nat.double_zero, Nat.double_succ] at eq; contradiction
707-    case succ m' =>
708-      congr
709-      /- At this point, the induction hypothesis `ih` does _not_ give us
710-      `n' = m'` -- there is an extra `succ` in the way -- so the goal is
711-      not provable. -/
712-      sorry
713-
714--- What went wrong?
715-
716--- The problem is that, at the point where we invoke the induction hypothesis,
717--- we have already introduced `m` into the context -- intuitively, we have
718--- told Lean, "Let's consider some particular `n` and `m`..." and we now have
719--- to prove that, if `double n = double m` for *these particular* `n` and `m`,
720--- then `n = m`.
721-
722--- The next tactic, `induction n` says to Lean: We are going to show the goal
723--- by induction on `n`. That is, we are going to prove, for *all* `n`, that
724--- the proposition
725-
726--- - `P n` = "if `double n = double m`, then `n = m`"
727-
728--- holds, by showing
729-
730--- - `P 0`
731-
732---   (i.e., "if `double 0 = double m` then `0 = m`") and
733-
734--- - `P n → P (.succ n)`
735-
736---   (i.e., "if `double n = double m` then `n = m`" implies "if
737---   `double (.succ n) = double m` then `.succ n = m`").
738-
739--- If we look closely at the second statement, it is saying something rather
740--- strange: that, for a *particular* `m`, if we know
741-
742--- - "if `double n = double m` then `n = m`"
743-
744--- then we can prove
745-
746--- - "if `double (.succ n) = double m` then `.succ n = m`".
747-
748--- To see why this is strange, let's think of a particular `m` -- say, `5`.
749--- The statement is then saying that, if we know
750-
751--- - `Q` = "if `double n = 10` then `n = 5`"
752-
753--- then we can prove
754-
755--- - `R` = "if `double (.succ n) = 10` then `.succ n = 5`".
756-
757--- But knowing `Q` doesn't give us any help at all with proving `R`! If we
758--- tried to prove `R` from `Q`, we would start with something like "Suppose
759--- `double (.succ n) = 10`..." but then we'd be stuck: knowing that
760--- `double (.succ n)` is `10` tells us nothing helpful about whether
761--- `double n` is `10` (indeed, it strongly suggests that `double n` is *not*
762--- `10`!!), so `Q` is useless.
763-
764--- Trying to carry out this proof by induction on `n` when `m` is already in
765--- the context doesn't work because we are then trying to prove a statement
766--- involving *every* `n` but just a *particular* `m`.
767-
768--- A successful proof of `double_injective` keeps `m` universally quantified
769--- in the goal statement at the point where the `induction` tactic is invoked
770--- on `n`.
771-
772-theorem double_injective : ∀ (n m : Nat),
773-    n.double = m.double →
774-    n = m := by
775-  intro n
776-  induction n
777-  case zero =>
778-    rw [Nat.double_zero]
779-    intro m eq
780-    cases m
781-    case zero => rfl
782-    case succ _ =>
783-      rw [Nat.double_succ] at eq
784-      contradiction
785-  case succ n' ih =>
786-  -- Notice that both the goal and the induction hypothesis are
787-  -- different this time: the goal asks us to prove something more
788-  -- general (i.e., we must prove the statement for _every_ `m`), but
789-  -- the induction hypothesis `ih` is correspondingly more flexible,
790-  -- allowing us to choose any `m` we like when we apply it.
791-  intro m eq
792-  -- Now we've introduced the assumption that `double n = double m`.
793-  -- Since we are doing a case analysis on `n`, we also need a case
794-  -- analysis on `m` to keep the two in sync.
795-  cases m
796-  case zero =>
797-    -- The 0 case is trivial:
798-    rw [Nat.double_zero, Nat.double_succ] at eq
799-    contradiction
800-  case succ m' =>
801-    congr
802-    -- Since we are now in the second branch of the `cases m`, the
803-    -- `m'` mentioned in the context is the predecessor of the `m` we
804-    -- started out talking about.  Since we are also in the `succ` branch of
805-    -- the induction, this is perfect: if we instantiate the generic `m`
806-    -- in the IH with the current `m'` (this instantiation is performed
807-    -- automatically by the `apply` in the next step), then `ih` gives
808-    -- us exactly what we need to finish the proof.
809-    apply ih; rw [Nat.double_succ, Nat.double_succ] at eq; injections
810-
811--- The thing to take away from all this is that you need to be careful, when
812--- using induction, that you are not trying to prove something too specific:
813--- When proving a property quantified over variables `n` and `m` by induction
814--- on `n`, it is sometimes crucial to leave `m` "generic."
815-

817--- `=`, follows the same pattern.

838--- The strategy of doing fewer `intros` before an `induction` to obtain a more
839--- general IH doesn't always work; sometimes some *rearrangement* of
840--- quantified variables is needed. Suppose, for example, that we wanted to
841--- prove `double_injective` by induction on `m` instead of `n`.
842-
843-theorem double_injective_take2_FAILED (n m : Nat) :
844-    n.double = m.double →
845-    n = m := by
846-  induction m
847-  case zero =>
848-    intro eq
849-    cases n
850-    case zero => rfl
851-    case succ =>
852-      rw [Nat.double_zero, Nat.double_succ] at eq
853-      contradiction
854-  case succ =>
855-    intro eq
856-    cases n
857-    case zero =>
858-      rw [Nat.double_zero, Nat.double_succ] at eq
859-      contradiction
860-    case succ =>
861-      congr
862-    -- We are stuck here, just like before.
863-      sorry
864-
865--- The problem is that, to do induction on `m`, we must first introduce `n`.
866-
867--- What can we do about this? One possibility is to rewrite the statement of
868--- the lemma so that `m` is quantified before `n`. This works, but it's not
869--- nice: We don't want to have to twist the statements of lemmas to fit the
870--- needs of a particular strategy for proving them! Rather we want to state
871--- them in the clearest and most natural way.
872-
873--- What we can do instead is to first introduce all the quantified variables
874--- and then explicitly generalize one or more of them The `generalizing`
875--- option for the `induction` tactic does this.
876-
877-theorem double_injective_take2 (n m : Nat) :
878-    n.double = m.double →
879-    n = m := by
880-  intro eq
881-  -- `n` and `m` are both in the context
882-  -- This lets us do induction on `m` and get a sufficiently general IH
883-  induction m generalizing n
884-  case zero =>
885-    cases n
886-    case zero => rfl
887-    case succ =>
888-      rw [Nat.double_zero, Nat.double_succ] at eq
889-      contradiction
890-  case succ _ ih =>
891-    cases n
892-    case zero =>
893-      rw [Nat.double_zero, Nat.double_succ] at eq
894-      contradiction
895-    case succ =>
896-      congr
897-      rw [Nat.double_succ, Nat.double_succ] at eq
898-      injections _ eq; exact ih _ eq
899-
900--- Let's look at an informal proof of this theorem. Note that the proposition
901--- we prove by induction leaves `n` quantified, corresponding to the use of
902--- generalize dependent in our formal proof.
903-
904--- *Theorem*: For any nats `n` and `m`, if `double n = double m`, then
905--- `n = m`.
906-
907--- *Proof*: Let `m` be a `Nat`. We prove by induction on `m` that, for any
908--- `n`, if `double n = double m` then `n = m`.
909-
910--- - First, suppose `m = 0`, and suppose `n` is a number such that
911---   `double n = double m`. We must show that `n = 0`.
912-
913---   Since `m = 0`, by the definition of `double` we have [double n = 0]. There
914---   are two cases to consider for `n`. If `n = 0` we are done, since
915---   `m = 0 = n`, as required. Otherwise, if `n = .succ n'` for some `n'`, we
916---   derive a contradiction: by the definition of `double`, we can calculate
917---   `double n = .succ (.succ (double n'))`, but this contradicts the assumption
918---   that `double n = 0`.
919-
920--- - Second, suppose `m = .succ m'` and that `n` is again a number such that
921---   `double n = double m`. We must show that `n = .succ m'`, with the induction
922---   hypothesis that for every number `s`, if [double s = double m'] then
923---   `s = m'`.
924-
925---   By the fact that `m = .succ m'` and the definition of `double`, we have
926---   `double n = .succ (.succ (double m'))`. There are two cases to consider for
927---   `n`.
928-
929---   If `n = 0`, then by definition `double n = 0`, a contradiction.
930-
931---   Thus, we may assume that `n = .succ n'` for some `n'`, and again by the
932---   definition of `double` we have
933---   `.succ (.succ (double n')) = .succ (.succ (double m'))`, which implies by
934---   injectivity that `double n' = double m'`. Instantiating the induction
935---   hypothesis with `n'` thus allows us to conclude that `n' = m'`, and it
936---   follows immediately that `.succ n' = .succ m'`. Since `.succ n' = n` and
937---   `.succ m' = m`, this is just what we wanted to show. []

939--- ## Rewriting with Conditional Statements
940-
941--- We'll use a boolean "less or equal" test on numbers, written `n ≤? m` (the
942--- library function `Nat.ble`), together with the fact that it commutes with
943--- successor on both sides.
944-
945-infix:52 " ≤? " => Nat.ble
946-
947-theorem zero_ble (m : Nat) : (0 ≤? m) = true := rfl
948-theorem succ_ble_succ (n m : Nat) : ((n + 1) ≤? (m + 1)) = (n ≤? m) := rfl
949-
950--- Suppose that we want to show that `add` is the inverse of `sub`. Since we
951--- are working with natural numbers, we need an assumption to prevent `sub`
952--- from truncating its result. With this assumption, the induction hypothesis
953--- becomes `forall m, n' ≤? m = true → (m - n') + n' = m`. The beginning of
954--- the proof uses techniques we have already seen -- in particular, notice how
955--- we induct on `n` before introducing `m`, so that the induction hypothesis
956--- becomes sufficiently general.
957-
958-theorem sub_add_ble : ∀ (n m : Nat),
959-    n ≤? m = true → (m - n) + n = m := by
960-  intro n
961-  induction n
962-  case zero =>
963-    intro m h; rw [add_zero]; cases m
964-    case zero => rfl
965-    case succ => rfl
966-  case succ n' ih =>
967-    intro m h; cases m
968-    case zero => contradiction
969-    case succ m' =>
970-      rw [succ_ble_succ] at h
971-      rw [succ_sub_succ, add_succ]
972-    -- At this point, we need to show `(m' - n') + n' + 1 = m' + 1`
973-    -- from the assumption `(n' <= m') = true`.  We could use the
974-    -- `have` tactic to prove `(m' - n') + n' = m'` from the IH.
975-    -- However, we can also just use `rw` directly...
976-      rw [ih]
977-      assumption
978-
979--- if we rewrite with a conditional statement of the form `P → a = b`, then
980--- Lean tries to rewrite with `a = b`, and then asks us to prove `P` in a new
981--- subgoal. If the statement has more than one assumption, then we get one
982--- subgoal for each assumption.

993--- ## Using `cases` on Compound Expressions
994-
995--- We have seen many examples where `cases` is used to perform case analysis
996--- of the value of some variable. Sometimes we need to reason by cases on the
997--- result of some *expression*. We can also do this with `cases`.
998-
999--- Here are some examples:
1000-
1001-def sillyfun (n : Nat) : Bool :=
1002-  if n == 3 then false
1003-  else if n == 5 then false
1004-  else false
1005-
1006-theorem sillyfun_false (n : Nat) :
1007-    sillyfun n = false := by
1008-  unfold sillyfun
1009-  cases (n == 3)
1010-  case false =>
1011-    dsimp; cases (n == 5)
1012-    case false => rfl
1013-    case true => rfl
1014-  case true => rfl
1015-
1016--- After unfolding `sillyfun` in the above proof, we find that we are stuck on
1017--- `if (n == 3) then ... else ...`. But either `n` is equal to `3` or it
1018--- isn't, so we can use `cases (n == 3)` to let us reason about the two cases.
1019-
1020--- In general, the `cases` tactic can be used to perform case analysis of the
1021--- results of arbitrary computations. If `e` is an expression whose type is
1022--- some inductively defined type `T`, then, for each constructor `c` of `T`,
1023--- `cases e` generates a subgoal in which all occurrences of `e` (in the goal
1024--- and in the context) are replaced by `c`.
1025-
1026--- ### Destructing Tuples
1027-
1028--- `cases` is useful when we are dealing with inductively defined types that
1029--- can be one thing or another; a `Bool` is either a `false` or a `true`, and
1030--- a `Nat` is either `0` or `succ n`. When we want more information about
1031--- inductively defined types that are products of multiple things, we instead
1032--- want a way to get the pieces of that value out from it.
1033-
1034--- When we have a value `v : α × β` in our context, we can get the first and
1035--- second projections of `v` using this tactic:
1036-
1037---   let ⟨a, β⟩ := v
1038-

1040-
1041--- Here is an implementation of the `unzip` function mentioned in chapter
1042--- Poly. We'll call it `split` so as not to confuse Lean.
1043-
1044-def split {α β : Type} (l : List (α × β)) : (List α) × (List β) :=
1045-  match l with
1046-  | [] => ([], [])
1047-  | (x, y) :: t =>
1048-    match split t with
1049-    | (lx, ly) => (x :: lx, y :: ly)
1050-

1052-
1053-theorem split_zip {α β : Type} (l : List (α × β)) l1 l2 :
1054-    split l = (l1, l2) →
1055-    zip l1 l2 = l := by
1056-  sorry

1058--- For example, suppose we define a function `sillyfun1` like this:
1059-
1060-def sillyfun1 (n : Nat) : Bool :=
1061-  if n == 3 then true
1062-  else if n == 5 then true
1063-  else false
1064-
1065--- Now suppose that we want to convince Lean that `sillyfun1 n` yields `true`
1066--- only when `n` is odd. If we start the proof like this (with no `h:` on the
1067--- `cases`)...
1068-
1069-example (n : Nat) :
1070-    sillyfun1 n = true →
1071-    n.odd = true := by
1072-  intro eq
1073-  unfold sillyfun1 at eq
1074-  cases (n == 3)
1075-  case false => sorry
1076-  case true => sorry
1077-
1078--- ... then we are stuck at this point because the context does not contain
1079--- enough information to prove the goal! Because `n == 3` appears in our
1080--- hypothesis, rather than in our goal, `cases (n == 3)` does not
1081--- automatically replace the expression with `false` or `true` like it did
1082--- during the proof of `sillyfun_false`. We want to add an equation to the
1083--- context that records which case we are in. This is precisely what the `h:`
1084--- qualifier does.
1085-
1086-theorem sillyfun1_odd (n : Nat) :
1087-    sillyfun1 n = true →
1088-    n.odd = true := by
1089-  intro eq
1090-  unfold sillyfun1 at eq
1091-  cases h : (n == 3)
1092-  case false =>
1093-    -- Now we have the same state as at the point where we got stuck
1094-    -- above, except that the context contains an extra equality
1095-    -- assumption, which is exactly what we need to make progress.
1096-    rw [h] at eq; dsimp at eq
1097-    cases h': (n == 5)
1098-    case false =>
1099-      rw [h'] at eq; dsimp at eq
1100-      contradiction
1101-    case true =>
1102-      apply beq_eq at h'
1103-      rw [h']; rfl
1104-      -- When we come to the second equality test in the body
1105-      -- of the function we are reasoning about, we can use
1106-      -- `h:` again in the same way, allowing us to finish the
1107-      -- proof.
1108-  case true =>
1109-    apply beq_eq at h
1110-    rw [h]; rfl

1118--- ## Review
1119-
1120--- We've now talked about many of Lean's most fundamental tactics. We'll
1121--- introduce a few more in the coming chapters, and later on we'll see some
1122--- more powerful *automation* tactics that make Lean help us with low-level
1123--- details. But basically we've got what we need to get work done.
1124-
1125--- Here are the ones we've seen:
1126-
1127--- - `intro`: move hypotheses/variables from goal to context
1128-
1129--- - `rfl`: finish the proof (when the goal looks like [e = e])
1130-
1131--- - `apply`: prove goal using a hypothesis, lemma, or constructor
1132-
1133--- - `apply... at H`: apply a hypothesis, lemma, or constructor to a hypothesis
1134---   in the context (forward reasoning)
1135-
1136--- - `apply... with...`: explicitly specify values for variables that cannot be
1137---   determined by pattern matching
1138-
1139--- - `replace h (x:= ...)`: refine a hypothesis by fixing some of its variables
1140-
1141--- - `dsimp`: simplify computations in the goal
1142-
1143--- - `dsimp at H`: ... or a hypothesis
1144-
1145--- - `rw`: use an equality hypothesis (or lemma) to rewrite the goal
1146-
1147--- - `rw ... at H`: ... or a hypothesis
1148-
1149--- - `symm`: changes a goal of the form `t=u` into `u=t`
1150-
1151--- - `symm at H`: changes a hypothesis of the form `t=u` into `u=t`
1152-
1153--- - `calc`: prove a goal about a transitive relation via a number of
1154---   intermediate steps
1155-
1156--- - `unfold`: replace a defined constant by its right-hand side in the goal
1157-
1158--- - `unfold... at H`: ... or a hypothesis
1159-
1160--- - `cases ...`: case analysis on values of inductively defined types
1161-
1162--- - `cases h:...`: specify the name of an equation to be added to the context,
1163---   recording the result of the case analysis
1164-
1165--- - `induction ...`: induction on values of inductively defined types
1166-
1167--- - `induction ... generalizing ...`: hold some variables general while doing
1168---   induction
1169-
1170--- - `injection ... with ...`: reason by injectivity on an equality between
1171---   values of inductively defined types
1172-
1173--- - `injections ... `: reason by injectivity on all the equalities in the
1174---   context
1175-
1176--- - `contradiction`: conclude a proof when there's a false hypothesis in the
1177---   context
1178-
1179--- - `have h : e := ... ` : introduce a "local lemma" `e` and call it `h`
1180-
1181--- - `congr`: change a goal of the form `f x = f y` into `x = y`
1182-
