1-import LF.SFLCompat
2-
3--- # Typeclasses
4-
5--- Chapter Poly introduced **parametric polymorphism**, declaring a type
6--- variable with no constraint on it:
7-
8-variable (α : Type)
9-
10--- This lets us work with a type like `List α`, writing functions like
11--- `List.reverse` and `List.length` and proofs like `List.length_reverse`,
12--- which use only the list's structure and never inspect any particular
13--- `a : α`.
14-
15--- Sometimes, though, we want less freedom: rather than leaving `α` completely
16--- generic, we want to partially specify its behavior. In Lean, this is done
17--- through a form of "ad hoc polymorphism" called **typeclasses**. The concept
18--- originated in Haskell and is analogous to features you may know from other
19--- languages, such as traits in Rust.
20-
21--- ## Why We Need Typeclasses
22-
23--- Consider the following function, which checks whether a natural number
24--- occurs in a list:
25-
26-def List.elem_nat (a : Nat) (xs : List Nat) : Bool :=
27-  match xs with
28-  | [] => false
29-  | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_nat a tl
30-
31-theorem List.elem_nat_nil (a : Nat) : [].elem_nat a = false := rfl
32-
33-theorem List.elem_nat_cons (a b : Nat) (xs : List Nat) :
34-    (b :: xs).elem_nat a = bif a == b then true else elem_nat a xs := rfl
35-
36-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 0
37-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 1
38-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 2
39-
40--- What if we want this to work for lists of *any* element type, not just
41--- `Nat`? Parametric polymorphism suggests simply replacing `Nat` with a type
42--- variable `α`, but that produces a puzzling error:
43-
44-sf_expect_failure
45-  def List.elem_poly {α : Type} (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
46-    match xs with
47-    | [] => false
48-    | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
49-
50--- Lean is trying to use typeclasses to work out how `==` should behave on a
51--- value of type `α`. We'll see exactly why shortly; for now, here's one way
52--- to sidestep the problem: have the caller supply the equality test to use.
53-
54-def List.elem_poly_eq {α : Type} (eq : α → α → Bool) (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
55-  match xs with
56-  | [] => false
57-  | b :: tl => bif eq a b then true else elem_poly_eq eq a tl
58-
59-#eval [0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0
60-
61--- This works, but it's tedious: every caller has to know, and remember to
62--- supply, the right equality function.
63-
64--- Typeclasses automate this — instead of the programmer passing the function
65--- explicitly, Lean searches for one and provides it on its own. We specify
66--- something we want Lean to search for by declaring a `class` with the needed
67--- function as a field; a `class` is like an interface in Java or a trait in
68--- Rust. Particular implementations of that class, different ones for
69--- different types, are called *instances*. For functions that would use such
70--- instances, we specify the name of the class in a *instance implicit* on the
71--- polymorphic variable that the instance's function applies to. This directs
72--- Lean to rely on the class inside the function, and to find and fill in the
73--- appropriate instance when the function is called.
74-
75--- Here is what this looks like for `List.elem_poly`:
76-
77-def List.elem_poly {α : Type} [BEq α] (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
78-  match xs with
79-  | [] => false
80-  | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
81-
82-theorem List.elem_poly_nil [BEq α] (a : α) : [].elem_poly a = false := rfl
83-
84-theorem List.elem_poly_cons [BEq α] (a b : α) (xs : List α) :
85-    (b :: xs).elem_poly a = bif a == b then true else elem_poly a xs := rfl
86-
87-#eval [0, 1].elem_poly 0
88-
89--- Comparing `List.elem_poly_eq` with `List.elem_poly`, we see three
90--- differences. First, `List.elem_poly_eq` takes an *explicit* parameter `eq`,
91--- whereas `List.elem_poly` specifies an instance implicit `[BEq α]`. The
92--- instance implicit indicates that an instance of `BEq` must be provided at
93--- call sites for the particular type `α` that is used. Second, whereas
94--- `List.elem_poly_eq` invokes parameter `eq` to test equality,
95--- `List.elem_poly` uses `==` instead. As Lists noted when we first used it,
96--- `==` on `Nat` comes from the `BEq` typeclass. Finally, whereas
97--- `[0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0` passes the equality function `Nat.beq`
98--- explicitly, in `[0, 1].elem_poly 0` Lean fills it in automatically based on
99--- the type `Nat` of the `List`.
100-
101--- Going back to the earlier version of `List.elem_poly`, without the instance
102--- implicit, we can now understand the error message: `α` was fully generic —
103--- so the `==` in its body would have needed to work for *every* type `α`, and
104--- no single `BEq` instance can do that. So Lean's search failed.
105-
106--- Now it is time to dig into the details of what we have seen so far. We'll
107--- see exactly how `[BEq α]` gets filled in below, starting with how to define
108--- a typeclass in the first place.
109-
110--- ## Defining Your Own Typeclasses
111-
112--- `BEq` comes from Lean's standard library. Let's define a typeclass of our
113--- own, to see the mechanism — classes, instances, and synthesis — that made
114--- `==` resolve automatically above.
115-
116--- Suppose we want a function that returns the first element of a list,
117--- defaulting to a given value if the list is empty. As with
118--- `List.elem_poly_eq` above, here is a version that makes the default value
119--- an explicit parameter:
120-
121-def List.headOr_ex {α : Type} (defaultValue : α) (xs : List α) : α :=
122-  match xs with
123-  | [] => defaultValue
124-  | hd :: _ => hd
125-
126-#eval [1, 2, 3].headOr_ex 0
127-#eval ([] : List Nat).headOr_ex 0
128-
129--- This works, but again it's tedious: every caller has to supply an element
130--- of `α` to default to, even when there's an obvious choice based on the type
131--- of the things in the list, like `0` for `Nat`.
132-
133--- Getting Lean to fill in `defaultValue` automatically takes two things. One
134--- is marking the parameter as "searchable," rather than something the caller
135--- always supplies explicitly. The other is giving Lean some information about
136--- what it should search *for*.
137-
138--- Considering the second problem first: The way to provide this information
139--- is to *name* the type-level concept we're after — the **default value** of
140--- a type. In particular, a `structure` (chapter Lists) is a good way to give
141--- a type-level concept a name; structures can also bundle together more than
142--- one piece of data, which will come in handy later, though we only need a
143--- single field here.
144-
145--- Considering the first problem: we need to mark this particular structure as
146--- one Lean should search for automatically — not every `structure`-typed
147--- argument should be.
148-
149--- Let's build up to what wewant in two steps: first the naming, as a plain
150--- `structure`; then the marking, by upgrading it to a `class`. Here's the
151--- structure — we'll put it in its own namespace so we can reuse the name
152--- `DefaultValue` for the class version below:
153-
154-namespace DefaultValueScratch
155-
156-structure DefaultValue (α : Type) where
157-  value : α
158-
159--- A value of type `DefaultValue Nat` picks out a particular `Nat` to serve as
160--- the type's default: it's built the same way any structure is, by supplying
161--- a `Nat` for the `value` field:
162-
163-def natDefault : DefaultValue Nat where
164-  value := 0
165-
166-example : natDefault.value = 0 := rfl
167-
168-end DefaultValueScratch
169-
170--- Now for the marking: we need to tell Lean that `DefaultValue` is the sort
171--- of structure it should search for automatically, the way it needs to for
172--- `List.headOr_ex`'s `defaultValue` argument. We do this by writing `class`
173--- in place of `structure`:
174-
175-class DefaultValue (α : Type) where
176-  value : α
177-
178--- We then provide values of this type a bit differently. Instead of `def`, we
179--- use `instance`:
180-
181-instance instDefaultValueNat : DefaultValue Nat where
182-  value := 0
183-
184--- Lean can now find this instance on its own, via **typeclass synthesis** (or
185--- **typeclass inference**) — the same process that found `BEq Nat` earlier.
186--- That means we can rewrite `List.headOr_ex` the same way we rewrote
187--- `List.elem_poly_eq` into `List.elem_poly` above, replacing the explicit
188--- `defaultValue` parameter with an instance implicit:
189-
190-def List.headOr {α : Type} [DefaultValue α] (xs : List α) : α :=
191-  match xs with
192-  | [] => DefaultValue.value
193-  | hd :: _ => hd
194-
195-#eval [1, 2, 3].headOr
196-#eval ([] : List Nat).headOr
197-
198-example : DefaultValue.value = (0 : Nat) := rfl
199-
200--- Notice that we refer to `DefaultValue.value` alone, with no instance named.
201--- Because the expression equates `DefaultValue.value` with the `Nat` `0`,
202--- Lean selects `instDefaultValueNat`, the instance for `DefaultValue Nat`. We
203--- know this because we are able to prove that `DefaultValue.value` is equal
204--- to `0`.
205-
206--- Let's declare a second instance, for `Int`, the type of integers
207--- `... -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...`:
208-
209-instance instDefaultValueInt : DefaultValue Int where
210-  value := -1
211-
212--- Now, Lean can infer instances for both types, including inside
213--- `List.headOr`:
214-
215-example : DefaultValue.value = (0 : Nat) := rfl
216-example : DefaultValue.value = (-1 : Int) := rfl
217-example : ([] : List Nat).headOr = 0 := rfl
218-example : ([] : List Int).headOr = -1 := rfl
219-
220--- Synthesis infers instances we could have specified explicitly:
221-
222-example : instDefaultValueNat.value = (0 : Nat) := rfl
223-example : instDefaultValueInt.value = (-1 : Int) := rfl
224-
225--- The option `pp.all` shows which instance Lean picked:
226-
227-set_option pp.all true in
228-#check (DefaultValue.value : Nat)
229-
230--- @DefaultValue.value Nat instDefaultValueNat : Nat
231-
232-set_option pp.all true in
233-#check (DefaultValue.value : Int)
234-
235--- @DefaultValue.value Int instDefaultValueInt : Int
236-
237--- This reveals `instDefaultValueNat` and `instDefaultValueInt` as the
238--- instances Lean picked. The `#synth` command runs the same search directly:
239-
240-#synth DefaultValue Nat
241-
242--- instDefaultValueNat
243-
244--- For a typeclass like `DefaultValue` that carries data — a term, such as the
245--- `1` above, rather than only proofs (which we will see below) — we expect at
246--- most one instance per type, so this search has a unique answer.
247-
248--- We'll put `DefaultValue`'s standard-library cousin, `Inhabited`, to work
249--- later in this chapter, when we define maps that need a default value for a
250--- generic type. First, though, let's go back to `List.elem_poly` and see how
251--- its `[BEq α]` argument actually gets resolved.
252-
253--- ## Using Typeclasses
254-
255--- Let's check what `==` meant for `List.elem_nat`, with notation display
256--- turned off:
257-
258-set_option pp.notation false in
259-#check 1 == 2
260-
261--- Rather than `Nat.beq`, `==` turns out to be notation for `BEq.beq`, a field
262--- of exactly the kind of typeclass we just learned to define:
263-
264--- class BEq (α : Type u) where
265---   /-- Boolean equality, notated as `a == b`. -/
266---   beq : α → α → Bool
267-
268--- Writing `a == b` makes Lean search for an **instance** of `BEq` for the
269--- type of `a` and `b`, the same way it searched for a `DefaultValue` instance
270--- above. For `Nat`, that instance is:
271-
272-instance (priority := low) : BEq Nat where
273-  beq := Nat.beq
274-
275--- This is the instance Lean supplies for `[BEq α]` when `List.elem_poly` is
276--- called on a `List Nat` — no different from Lean choosing
277--- `instDefaultValueNat` for `DefaultValue.value` earlier when it was equated
278--- with `(1 : Nat)`.
279-
280--- ### Exercise (1 star): List.elem_poly_eq_elem_nat ⭐
281-
282--- Prove that `List.elem_poly` agrees with `List.elem_nat` when specialized to
283--- natural numbers.
284-
285-theorem List.elem_poly_eq_elem_nat (xs : List Nat) (n : Nat) : xs.elem_poly n = xs.elem_nat n := by
286-  sorry
287-
288--- ## Proof-Carrying Typeclasses
289-
290--- The above examples enforce no conditions on the data an instance may carry
291--- — any value of the right type will do. But sometimes enforcing constraints
292--- on data is useful. For example, suppose we want to specify that a type has
293--- not just a single element, but two. Here is a first attempt:
294-
295-sf_experiment
296-  class HasTwoIncomplete (α : Type) where
297-    one : α
298-    two : α
299-
300--- Unfortunately, this specification isn't precise because it allows `one` and
301--- `two` to refer to the same term. Fortunately, Lean's typeclasses can carry
302--- proofs along with data, so we can write the following to enforce that `one`
303--- and `two` are distinct.
304-
305-class HasTwo (α : Type) where
306-  one : α
307-  two : α
308-  one_neq_two : one ≠ two
309-
310--- Declaring instances works in much the same way as before, except that now
311--- the `HasTwo.one_neq_two` field requires a proof:
312-
313-instance : HasTwo Nat where
314-  one := 1
315-  two := 2
316-  one_neq_two := by intro contra; contradiction
317-
318--- In most languages that support typeclasses (or traits) it is not possible
319--- to formally enforce laws such as `one_neq_two`. Thus it falls to the author
320--- to check, informally, that any required invariants are satisfied, which can
321--- lead to bugs.
322-
323--- ### Exercise (1 star): HasThree ⭐
324-
325--- Following the pattern of `DefaultValue` and `HasTwo`, define a class
326--- `HasThree` that specifies a type with at least three distinct elements, and
327--- give an instance of it for `Nat`.
328-
329-class HasThree (α : Type) where
330-  one : α
331-  two : α
332-  three : α
333-  one_neq_two : one ≠ two
334-  -- FILL IN HERE
335-
336-instance : HasThree Nat where
337-  one := 1
338-  two := 2
339-  three := 3
340-  one_neq_two := sorry
341-  -- FILL IN HERE
342-
343--- ## Maps
344-
345--- *Maps* (or "dictionaries") are ubiquitous data structures both in ordinary
346--- programming and in the theory of programming languages; we're going to need
347--- them in many places in later volumes.
348-
349--- We'll define two flavors of maps: *total maps*, which include a "default"
350--- element to be returned when a key being looked up doesn't exist, and
351--- *partial maps*, which instead return an option to indicate success or
352--- failure. Partial maps are defined in terms of total maps, using `none` as
353--- the default element.
354-
355--- ### Key and Value Types
356-
357--- To define maps, we first need a type for the keys that we will use to index
358--- into our maps and a type for the values the maps return. Instead of
359--- choosing concrete types for these, we will use type variables.
360-
361-variable {α : Type} {β : Type} [BEq α] [ReflBEq α] [LawfulBEq α]
362-
363-set_option linter.unusedSectionVars false
364-
365--- Here, `α` is the type of the keys and `β` the corresponding values. In
366--- addition to `BEq`, which we have already seen, the key type `α` requires
367--- instances of the `ReflBEq` and `LawfulBEq` typeclasses:
368-
369--- /-- `ReflBEq α` says that the `BEq` implementation is reflexive. -/
370--- class ReflBEq (α) [BEq α] : Prop where
371---   /-- `==` is reflexive, that is, `(a == a) = true`. -/
372---   protected rfl {a : α} : a == a
373-
374--- /--
375--- A Boolean equality test coincides with propositional equality.
376-
377--- In other words:
378---  * `a == b` implies `a = b`.
379---  * `a == a` is true.
380--- -/
381--- class LawfulBEq (α : Type u) [BEq α] : Prop extends ReflBEq α where
382---   /-- If `a == b` evaluates to `true`, then `a` and `b` are equal in the logic. -/
383---   eq_of_beq : {a b : α} → a == b → a = b
384-
385--- These classes refine `BEq`, specifying that (`==`) is reflexive and
386--- coincides with proposition equality `=`.
387-
388--- We place no constraints on the value type `β`.
389-
390--- ### Total Maps
391-
392--- The Lists chapter introduced a partial map abstraction, `PartialMap`, with
393--- a `find` function for lookup, based on lists of key-value pairs. Here, we
394--- are going to build a map abstraction using functions instead. The advantage
395--- of this representation is that it offers a more *extensional* view of maps,
396--- as we saw with functions in the Logic chapter: two maps that respond to
397--- every query in the same way will be represented as exactly the same
398--- function, rather than just as "equivalent" list structures. This simplifies
399--- proofs that use maps.
400-
401--- Instead of using functions directly, we encapsulate them inside a
402--- `structure` which we call `TotalMap`. Intuitively, a total map just
403--- contains a function `inner` from a key of type `α` to a value of type `β`.
404-
405-structure TotalMap (α : Type) (β : Type) where
406-  inner : α → β
407-
408-namespace TotalMap
409-
410--- In order to declare a default value of `β` we will use the `Inhabited`
411--- typeclass, which is the standard library's implementation of our
412--- `DefaultValue` example from above:
413-
414-variable [Inhabited β]
415-
416--- The function `TotalMap.empty` yields an empty total map, given a default
417--- element; this map always returns the default element when applied to any
418--- key.
419-
420-def empty : TotalMap α β where
421-  inner := fun _ ↦ default
422-
423--- Just as declaring `BEq`/`DefaultValue` instances above hooked `==` and
424--- `DefaultValue.value` up to our types, we can declare an instance of the
425--- standard library's `EmptyCollection` typeclass to associate `∅` with this
426--- empty map.
427-
428-instance : EmptyCollection (TotalMap α β) where
429-  emptyCollection := TotalMap.empty
430-
431-theorem empty_def : (∅ : TotalMap α β) = { inner := fun _ ↦ default } := by rfl
432-
433--- Here, for example, is an empty map that takes `Nat` keys to `Nat` values:
434-
435-def emptyNatMap : TotalMap Nat Nat := ∅
436-
437--- #### Getting Elements
438-
439--- While `TotalMap`s happen to be implemented as functions under the hood, we
440--- would prefer not to expose this fact in its public interface. Accordingly,
441--- we define new operations for querying and updating mappings. As a first
442--- attempt at a query operation, playing the role that `find` played for the
443--- Lists chapter's list-based maps, we could define a function `get` for
444--- getting the value associated with a key:
445-
446-def get (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) := m.inner a
447-
448-/-- This exposes implementation-specific details of `TotalMap`.
449-Avoid using this outside the `TotalMap` namespace. -/
450-theorem get_def {m : TotalMap α β} {a : α} : m.get a = m.inner a := by rfl
451-
452-example : emptyNatMap.get 2 = 0 := by rfl
453-
454--- Here is an example that uses the API lemmas `empty_def` and `get_def`:
455-
456-example {n : Nat} : emptyNatMap.get n = 0 := by
457-  rewrite [get_def, emptyNatMap, empty_def, Nat.default_eq_zero]
458-  rfl
459-
460--- In the above example, we use `rewrite` and `rfl` instead of the usual `rw`
461--- to highlight something interesting. After the rewrites in this proof, we
462--- end up with a goal that looks like `{ inner := fun x => 0 }.inner n = 0`,
463--- which we can solve with `rfl`. This is because the projection `.inner` on a
464--- structure of the form `{ inner := x }` is definitionally equal to `x`.
465-
466--- `get` is the public API counterpart to `inner` which is an
467--- implementation-specific detail of `TotalMap`. Because `get_def` "peeks"
468--- through the abstraction, it should be used sparingly, and only inside the
469--- `TotalMap` namespace.
470-
471--- To make element-getting more convenient, let's define notation so we can
472--- write `emptyNatMap[2]` rather than `emptyNatMap.get`. We could notate `get`
473--- directly — we'll do exactly that for `update` below — but here we'll
474--- instead make "getting an element" its own typeclass, `MyGetElem`, and
475--- notate it. Doing so means `m[a]` resolves to `MyGetElem.getElem m a` for
476--- any type with a `MyGetElem` instance, not just `TotalMap`.
477-
478--- Using typeclasses to define notation is typical in Lean when the same
479--- notation is useful for many different types. We have seen the approach
480--- already with `==`: writing `a == b` is notation for `BEq.beq`, resolved by
481--- instance search for whatever type `a` and `b` have. We also just saw
482--- overloaded notation for `EmptyCollection` above, where `∅` is notation for
483--- `EmptyCollection.emptyCollection`. Our typeclass `MyGetElem` is a simpler
484--- version of the standard library's `GetElem` typeclass, which has many
485--- instances such as `Array`, `List`, and `Vector`. We develop it to
486--- illustrate the notation-as-typeclass approach.
487-
488-end TotalMap
489-
490--- The `MyGetElem` typeclass takes three type parameters: the map
491--- implementation, its keys, and its values.
492-
493-class MyGetElem (coll : Type) (idx : Type) (elem : outParam Type) where
494-  getElem (xs : coll) (i : idx) : elem
495-
496--- (Don't worry about the `outParam` qualifier; it is a hint to Lean that
497--- helps typeclass inference.)
498-
499--- The appropriate instance of `MyGetElem` for our `TotalMap` is:
500-
501-variable [Inhabited β]
502-instance : MyGetElem (TotalMap α β) α β where
503-  getElem m a := m.get a
504-
505--- Now we can associate the bracket syntax with `MyGetElem.getElem`. We've
506--- defined custom notation before — `::` and `[...]` for lists (chapter Lists,
507--- including an `app_unexpander` for printing `[...]`-notation lists back
508--- out), or `+`/`*`/`==` for arithmetic — but always with `infixl`/`infixr` or
509--- `scoped macro`; this is the first time we reach for the more general
510--- `notation`/`macro_rules` forms for getting the `m[a]` syntax to work.
511-
512--- Don't worry about following the mechanism in detail — the `macro_rules` and
513--- the `app_unexpander` below are minor technicalities. However, if you do
514--- wish to learn more, Chapter 5 and 6 of [Metaprogramming in Lean
515--- 4](https://leanprover-community.github.io/lean4-metaprogramming-book/)
516--- contain more detail.
517-
518-namespace MyGetElem
519-
520-scoped macro_rules | `($xs[$i]) => ``(getElem $xs $i)
521-
522-@[app_unexpander getElem]
523-def unexpandGetElem : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander
524-  | `($_ $xs $i) => `($xs[$i])
525-  | _ => throw ()
526-end MyGetElem
527-
528-open scoped MyGetElem
529-
530--- Since the standard library already declares the `x[i]` syntax for
531--- `GetElem`, we only need to define the `macro_rules`, not the `notation` as
532--- we have done previously. It's scoped since we don't want to override the
533--- default `GetElem` everywhere, but only when `open scoped MyGetElem` is in
534--- force.
535-
536--- Since we provided a `MyGetElem` instance for `TotalMap`, we can now use the
537--- notation `m[a]` to access elements of a map `m`.
538-
539-namespace TotalMap
540-
541-theorem getElem_def (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m[a] = m.get a := by rfl
542-
543-example : emptyNatMap[1] = default := by rfl
544-
545-example {n : Nat} : emptyNatMap[n] = 0 := by
546-  rw [getElem_def, get_def, emptyNatMap, empty_def, Nat.default_eq_zero]
547-
548--- We want the public API of `TotalMap` to use the `m[a]` notation instead of
549--- `m.get a` so we provide the reverse direction of `getElem_def` as a `simp`
550--- lemma; the `m[a]` notation is the `TotalMap` API's `simp` normal form.
551-
552-@[simp]
553-theorem get_eq_getElem (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m.get a = m[a] := by rfl
554-
555-example {n : Nat} : emptyNatMap.get n = emptyNatMap[n] := by
556-  simp
557-
558--- This design minimizes the need to use `getElem_def` outside concrete
559--- examples (which are typically solvable with `rfl` anyways).
560-
561--- #### Updating Elements
562-
563--- Now we turn to the `update` function, which takes a map `m`, a key `a`, and
564--- a value `b` and returns a new map that takes `a` to `b` and takes every
565--- other key to whatever `m` does. We do this by wrapping a new map function
566--- around the old one.
567-
568-def update (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) : TotalMap α β where
569-  inner := fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a']
570-
571--- For example, we can build a map taking `String` to `Bool`, where `"foo"`
572--- and `"bar"` are mapped to `true` and every other key is mapped to `false`,
573--- like this:
574-
575-def exampleMap :=
576-  (∅ : TotalMap String Bool)
577-    |>.update "foo" true
578-    |>.update "bar" true
579-
580--- Here `|>` is Lean's **pipe** notation: `x |>.f y` means `x.f y`, letting us
581--- chain a sequence of function or method calls left to right without nested
582--- parentheses.
583-
584--- We also introduce a notation for updating maps — this time, rather than
585--- going through a typeclass and its own `notation`/`macro_rules` machinery as
586--- we did for `MyGetElem`, we write a `notation` that references
587--- `TotalMap.update` directly. Unlike indexing, `update` doesn't need to work
588--- generically across container types (there's no standard-library operation
589--- like `GetElem` that we're mirroring here), so the simpler, direct route
590--- suffices.
591-
592-notation a:55 " →ₜ " b:55 " ; " m:55 => TotalMap.update m a b
593-
594-/-- This exposes implementation-specific details of `TotalMap`.
595-Avoid using this outside the `TotalMap` namespace. Prefer `update_apply` if possible. -/
596-theorem update_def (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) :
597-  a →ₜ b ; m = { inner := fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a'] } := by rfl
598-
599-theorem update_apply (m : TotalMap α β) (a a' : α) (b : β) :
600-  (a →ₜ b ; m)[a'] = bif a == a' then b else m[a'] := by rfl
601-
602--- We can omit the map from the notation when we want it to be empty:
603-
604-notation a:55 " →ₜ " b:55 => TotalMap.update ∅ a b
605-
606--- The `examplemap` above can now be defined as follows:
607-
608-def exampleMap' : TotalMap String Bool := "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true ; ∅
609-def exampleMap'' : TotalMap String Bool := "bar" →ₜ true ; "foo" →ₜ true
610-
611-example : exampleMap = exampleMap' := by rfl
612-example : exampleMap' = exampleMap'' := by rfl
613-
614-example : exampleMap'["bar"] = true := by rfl
615-example : exampleMap'["foo"] = true := by rfl
616-example : exampleMap'["quux"] = false := by rfl
617-
618--- Let's also see a couple of examples of working with updated maps using
619--- rewrites:
620-
621-example : exampleMap'["bar"] = true := by
622-  rw [exampleMap', update_apply, BEq.rfl, cond_true]
623-
624-example : exampleMap'["foo"] = true := by
625-  rw [exampleMap', update_apply, show ("bar" == "foo") = false by simp, cond_false]
626-  rw [update_apply, BEq.rfl, cond_true]
627-
628-example : exampleMap'["quux"] = false := by
629-  rw [exampleMap', update_apply, show ("bar" == "quux") = false by simp, cond_false]
630-  rw [update_apply, show ("foo" == "quux") = false by rfl, cond_false]
631-  rw [empty_def, getElem_def, get_def, Bool.default_bool]
632-
633--- When we use maps in later volumes, we'll need several fundamental facts
634--- about how they behave.
635-
636--- Even if you don't work the following exercises, make sure you thoroughly
637--- understand the statements of the lemmas!
638-
639--- (Some of the proofs require the functional extensionality axiom `funext`,
640--- discussed in the Logic chapter.)
641-
642--- First, the empty map returns its default element for all keys:
643-
644-@[simp]
645-theorem getElem_empty (a : α) : (∅ : TotalMap α β)[a] = default := by
646-  rw [empty_def, getElem_def, get_def]
647-
648--- Notice that in the example `exampleMap'["quux"] = false` the last rewrite
649--- is effectively just `getElem_empty`.
650-

890--- Updating a partial map at a key means storing a `some` value there. To
891--- update, we create a new partial map from `a →ₜ some b ; m.toTotal` by
892--- wrapping it in angle brackets, i.e. using the anonymous constructor syntax.

894--- also introduce a similar notation for it as for total maps.

986--- One last thing: for partial maps, it's convenient to introduce a notion of
987--- map inclusion, stating that all the entries in one map are also present in
988--- another. Lean already has notation for this — `m₁ ⊆ m₂` — which we get by
989--- supplying a `HasSubset` instance.
990-
991-def Subset (m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β) : Prop :=
992-  ∀ (a : α) (b : β), m₁[a] = some b → m₂[a] = some b
993-
994-instance : HasSubset (PartialMap α β) where
995-  Subset := PartialMap.Subset
996-
997-theorem subset_def (m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β) :
998-    m₁ ⊆ m₂ ↔ (∀ (a : α) (b : β), m₁[a] = some b → m₂[a] = some b) := .rfl
999-
1000--- We can then show that map update preserves map inclusion, that is:
1001-
1002-theorem update_subset (m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) (h : m₁ ⊆ m₂) :
1003-    (a →ₚ b ; m₁) ⊆ (a →ₚ b ; m₂) := by
1004-  rw [subset_def] at h ⊢
1005-  intro a' b' hb
1006-  by_cases ha : a = a'
1007-  · subst ha
1008-    rw [update_eq] at hb ⊢
1009-    exact hb
1010-  · rw [update_neq ha] at hb ⊢
1011-    exact h a' b' hb
1012-
1013-end PartialMap

1026-@[irreducible]

1028-| 0 => true
1029-| 1 => false
1030-| n + 2 => isEven n
1031-
1032-@[irreducible]
1033-def double : Nat → Nat
1034-| 0 => 0
1035-| n + 1 => double n + 2

1037-section
1038-
1039-unseal isEven
1040-unseal double
1041-
1042-theorem isEven_zero : isEven 0 = true := rfl
1043-theorem isEven_one : isEven 1 = false := rfl
1044-theorem isEven_succ_succ (n : Nat) : isEven (n + 2) = isEven n := rfl
1045-
1046-theorem double_zero : double 0 = 0 := by rfl
1047-theorem double_succ (n : Nat) : double (n + 1) = double n + 2 := rfl

1049-end

1051-def Even (n : Nat) := ∃ m, n = double m
1052-
1053-theorem isEven_succ (n : Nat) : isEven (n + 1) = ! isEven n := by
1054-  induction n with
1055-  | zero =>
1056-    rewrite [Nat.zero_add, isEven_zero, isEven_one]
1057-    rfl
1058-  | succ n ih =>
1059-    rewrite [isEven_succ_succ, ih, Bool.not_not]
1060-    rfl
1061-
1062--- We've seen two different ways of expressing logical claims in Lean: with
1063--- booleans (of type `Bool`), and with propositions (of type `Prop`).
1064-
1065--- Here are the key differences between `Bool` and `Prop`:
1066-
1067--- - ⠀
1068--- - `Bool`
1069--- - `Prop`
1070--- - decidable?
1071--- - yes
1072--- - no
1073--- - useable with `match`?
1074--- - yes
1075--- - no
1076--- - works with `rewrite` tactic?
1077--- - no
1078--- - yes
1079-
1080--- The crucial difference between the two worlds is decidability. Every
1081--- (closed) Lean expression of type `Bool` can be simplified in a finite
1082--- number of steps to either `true` or `false` — i.e., there is a terminating
1083--- mechanical procedure for deciding whether or not it is true.
1084-
1085--- This means that, for example, the type `Nat → Bool` is inhabited only by
1086--- functions that, given a `Nat`, always yield either `true` or `false` in
1087--- finite time; and this, in turn, means (by a standard computability
1088--- argument) that there is no function in `Nat → Bool` that checks whether a
1089--- given number is the code of a terminating Turing machine.
1090-
1091--- By contrast, the type `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1092--- mathematical propositions; in particular, the type `Nat → Prop` does
1093--- contain functions representing properties like "the nth Turing machine
1094--- halts." The second row in the table follows directly from this essential
1095--- difference. To evaluate a pattern match (or conditional) on a boolean, we
1096--- need to know whether the scrutinee evaluates to `true` or `false`; this
1097--- only works for `Bool`, not `Prop`.
1098-
1099--- The third row highlights an important practical difference: equality
1100--- functions like `Nat.beq` that return a boolean cannot be used directly to
1101--- justify rewriting with the rewrite tactic; propositional equality is
1102--- required for this. Since `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1103--- properties, we have two options when we want to formalize a property that
1104--- happens to be decidable: we can express it either as a boolean computation
1105--- or as a function into Prop.
1106-
1107--- As an example, we can write
1108-
1109-unseal isEven in
1110-example : isEven 42 := rfl
1111-
1112--- or that there exists some `k` such that `42 = double k`.
1113-
1114-unseal double in
1115-example : Even 42 := by exists 21
1116-
1117--- Of course, it would be deeply strange if these two characterizations of
1118--- evenness did not describe the same set of natural numbers!
1119-
1120--- Fortunately, they do! To prove this, we first need two helper lemmas.
1121-
1122-theorem even_double (k : Nat) : isEven (double k) = true := by
1123-  induction k with
1124-  | zero =>
1125-    rewrite [double_zero, isEven_zero]
1126-    rfl
1127-  | succ n ih =>
1128-    rewrite [double_succ, isEven_succ_succ]
1129-    exact ih
1130-
1131--- ### Exercise (3 stars): isEven_double_exists ⭐⭐⭐
1132-
1133-theorem isEven_double_exists (n : Nat) :
1134-    ∃ k, n = bif isEven n then double k else double k + 1 := by sorry
1135-
1136--- Now the main theorem:
1137-
1138-theorem isEven_iff_Even {n : Nat} : isEven n = true ↔ Even n where
1139-  mp h := by
1140-    have ⟨k, hk⟩ := isEven_double_exists n
1141-    rewrite [h, cond_true] at hk
1142-    subst hk
1143-    exists k
1144-  mpr h := by
1145-    obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := h
1146-    subst hk
1147-    exact even_double k
1148-
1149--- In view of this theorem, we can say that the boolean computation `isEven n`
1150--- is reflected in the truth of the proposition `∃ k, n = double k`.
1151-
1152--- Similarly, to state that two numbers n and m are equal, we can say either
1153-
1154--- - that `n == m` returns `true`, or
1155--- - that `n = m`
1156-
1157--- Again, these two notions are equivalent:
1158-
1159-example (n₁ n₂ : Nat) : n₁ == n₂ ↔ n₁ = n₂ := beq_iff_eq
1160-
1161--- So what should we do in situations where some claim could be formalized as
1162--- either a proposition or a boolean computation? Which should we choose?
1163-
1164--- In general, both can be useful. Which we choose has to do with the
1165--- *computational* nature of Lean's core language, which is designed so that
1166--- every function it expresses is total, and by default computable unless we
1167--- explicit indicate otherwise. As an example, consider trying to write a
1168--- function `α → α → Bool` checking for equality on an arbitrary type:
1169-
1170--- Lean will complain here that it cannot find an instance of `Decidable`.
1171--- This typeclass
1172-
1173--- is the way that we express in Lean that a given proposition is decidable.
1174--- This is the generalization of our observation that `isEven_iff_Even` was
1175--- reflecting a proof between boolean and propositional equality. In fact, we
1176--- can use this theorem to directly construct a `Decidable` instance
1177-
1178-instance (n : Nat) : Decidable (Even n) := decidable_of_decidable_of_iff isEven_iff_Even
1179-
1180--- Now we are able to complete such proofs by computation using the `decide`
1181--- tactic:
1182-
1183-section
1184-unseal isEven
1185-

1195--- In general, Lean will try to use typeclass synthesis with `Decidable` in
1196--- order to determine when it is appropriate to use `Prop` and `Bool`
1197--- interchangeably. For instance, while our example `eq` failed above while
1198--- trying to use propositional equality `=` in the condition of an `if`
1199--- statement, we are allowed to write
1200-
1201-def nat_eq (m n : Nat) : Bool := if m = n then true else false
1202-
1203--- Why is this allowed? It is precisely because equality of natural numbers is
1204--- decidable, and Lean makes use of this fact. If we print this definition
1205--- with notation unset, we would find that it is using `instDecidableEqNat`
1206-
1207-set_option pp.all true in
1208-#print nat_eq
1209-
1210--- which proves that this equality is decidable.
1211-
1212--- This is only half the story however: while Lean's core theory enables this
1213--- computation, Lean is also often used in applications where we don't care
1214--- about computability, such as pure mathematics. In particular, it is
1215--- possible to write a function for arbitrary equality:
1216-
1217-sf_experiment
1218-  open scoped Classical in
1219-  noncomputable def eq {α : Type} (a₁ a₂ : α) := if a₁ = a₂ then true else false
1220-  
1221-  set_option pp.all true in
1222-  #print eq
1223-
1224--- But we have indicated to Lean, using the `noncomputable` keyword and
1225--- `Classical` namespace, that we are *not* interested in computation. What is
1226--- happening in the background is that this allows typeclass synthesis to find
1227--- the scoped instance `Classical.propDecidable`, which makes use of the axiom
1228--- of choice to provide a proof that all propositions are *classically*
1229--- decidable. This sort of definition is suitable for use with proofs, but is
1230--- not allowed to be used in conjunction with computational features of Lean
1231--- such as the `decide` tactic or the `#eval` command.

6--- # UsingLean: Using the full power of a proof assistant
7-

13-
14--- ## More powerful Natural Numbers
15-
16--- Until now, we have been working with our own custom natural numbers, using
17--- the `Nat` type that we defined in `Basics.lean`.
18-
19--- However, Lean has a built-in type of natural numbers, which is more
20--- powerful and comes with many useful features. They are very slightly
21--- different from our custom `Nat`, but these differences are mostly
22--- superficial. The built-in natural numbers are defined in the `Init` module,
23--- which is automatically imported by Lean. We will refer to them as `Nat` as
24--- well, but they are not the same as the `Nat` we defined in `Basics.lean`.
25-
26--- In Lean, programmers and mathematicians don't re-prove the basic properties
27--- of natural numbers from scratch, nor do they tend to write out `rewrite`
28--- steps for basic properties of natural numbers by hand.
29-
30-section long_example
31-open NatPlayground.Nat
32-
33--- Previously, we did computation like this...
34-
35-theorem test_mult1' : (two * two : NatPlayground.Nat) = four := by
36-  rewrite [two_eq_succ_one, one_eq_succ_zero]
37-  rewrite [mul_succ, mul_succ, mul_zero]
38-  rewrite [add_succ, add_succ, add_zero]
39-  rewrite [add_succ, add_succ, add_zero]
40-  rfl
41-end long_example
42-
43--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, NOW):
44---     The info viewed in the InfoView during this proof is kind of mysterious
45---     (to me) here. Have we already given people enough help to understand it
46---     here?
47-
48--- This approach is useful in a textbook for understanding the structure of
49--- natural numbers and for providing early practice with writing proofs. But
50--- it is also tedious in the long term.
51-
52--- Instead of doing this, programmers and mathematicians use the built-in
53--- `Nat` and the powerful features of Lean to *automatically* prove properties
54--- about natural numbers and to compute with them.
55-
56-theorem test_mult1_nat : (3 * 3 : Nat) = 9 := by
57-  rfl
58-
59--- The annotation `: Nat` tells Lean that we are using its built-in `Nat`
60--- type.
61-
62--- In this chapter we will learn how to use the built-in `Nat` and some
63--- powerful features for computing with and proving properties about natural
64--- numbers. Specifically, we will learn about `dsimp`, `calc`, and `simp`
65--- annotations, which enable more powerful and concise proofs.
66-
67--- In fact, from now on, we will use the built-in `Nat` type and its powerful
68--- features, writing `Nat.<theorem>` to reference Lean's version of
69--- `<theorem>`.
70-
71--- ### `rfl` and computation with `Nat`
72-
73--- With Lean's `Nat`, much of the computation happens automatically, and `rfl`
74--- suffices to close any equality of computation on literals.
75-
76-theorem complicated_computation : (2 * 3 + 4 * 5 : Nat) * 6 = 156 := by
77-  rfl
78-
79--- This quickly becomes necessary, as natural numbers quickly get large!
80-
81--- Of course, `rfl` can't close more complicated goals where the values of the
82--- terms are unknown.
83-
84-theorem rfl_not_enough (n m : Nat) (h : n = m) : n = m := by
85-  -- rfl will not work here!
86-  /- First rewrite the goal with `h`; then the two sides are identical. -/
87-  rewrite [h]
88-  rfl
89-
90--- The same proof can be written more compactly with `rw`. In this example,
91--- `rw [h]` rewrites with `h` and then closes the resulting reflexive goal.
92-
93-theorem rfl_not_enough' (n m : Nat) (h : n = m) : n = m := by
94-  rw [h]
95-
96--- We will continue to show more powerful tools for manipulating the context
97--- and goal of a proof to bring them closer to what can be solved with `rfl`.
98-
99--- ## Using the Standard Library
100-
101--- As part of using Lean's standard `Nat` type, we will also begin using
102--- theorems about `Nat`s from the standard library. Because we did not write
103--- or prove these theorems ourselves, however, we may not know all the
104--- available theorems off the top of our heads.
105-
106--- Lean provides a few ways to search through the standard library to find
107--- theorems that may be useful during a particular proof. The first such way
108--- is the `exact?` tactic. This tactic searches the standard library for a
109--- theorem that can be applied, along with the hypotheses in the context, to
110--- exactly close the current goal.
111-
112-example (a b : Nat) : a + b = b + a := by
113-  /- this will suggest that we use `exact Nat.add_comm a b` to close this goal -/
114-  exact?
115-
116--- If you are using the Lean 4 extension in VSCode, the InfoView will have a
117--- blue `[apply]` button that shows the suggested theorem to close the goal.
118--- Alternatively, VSCode may show an inline suggestion (light bulb) button
119--- above the `exact?`. You can click either of these buttons to replace the
120--- occurrence of `exact?` with the tactic it found to complete the proof;
121--- idiomatic Lean does not leave `exact?` tactics (or any other `?` tactics,
122--- as we will see shortly) in the finished versions of proofs and instead
123--- replaces them with the tactics they found during search.
124-
125--- The `exact?` tactic is useful when we just need a single library theorem to
126--- get us over the finish line of a proof, but it is not so helpful when we
127--- are deep in the middle of a proof or are wondering how to get started on
128--- one. Luckily, there are other tactics that will help us with this.
129-
130--- The `rw?` tactic works like `exact?`, except that it searches for any
131--- theorems that you could use to rewrite the current goal.
132-
133-example (a b : Nat) : a + b = b + a := by
134-  /- this will suggest that we use `rw [Nat.add_comm]` to close this goal -/
135-  rw?
136-
137--- However, unlike `exact?`, just because `rw?` suggests a theorem to you does
138--- not automatically imply that it will be useful. In the example below, many
139--- of the theorems `rw?` suggests will not progress towards completing the
140--- proof; you will need to carefully look through its suggestions to see which
141--- ones seem useful. We strongly recommend against blindly using `rw?` and
142--- accepting its suggestions without due consideration! You will find this a
143--- very slow and frustrating way to write proofs. Instead, we suggest figuring
144--- out what you would like your next step to be, conceptually, and then using
145--- `rw?` to search for a theorem that implements it. If no such theorem
146--- exists, that may be a sign that you need to prove it yourself.
147-
148-example (n m q : Nat) :
149-   (n + m) + q = m + (n + q) := by
150-  -- lots of suggestions to look through here!
151-  rw?
152-  sorry
153-
154--- Prove the following theorems about `Nat`s. You should not need induction
155--- for any of these; you can find the theorems you need using `rw?` and
156--- `exact?`.
157-
158-theorem mul_three (p : Nat) :
159-    3 * p = p + p + p := by
160-  sorry
161-
162-theorem mul_three_beq (p : Nat) :
163-    (3 * p == p + p + p) = true := by
164-  sorry
165-
166--- ## Structuring proofs with `calc`
167-
168--- In Lean proofs, long `rw` chains are useful, but they are sometimes hard to
169--- read because the intermediate goals are invisible. Furthermore, sometimes
170--- we *know* exactly how we want to manipulate the terms of a proof, but don't
171--- want to have the tactics like `add_comm` and `add_assoc` "guess" which
172--- subterms to rewrite.
173-
174--- The `calc` tactic writes down the intermediate goals of a proof, and allows
175--- us to specify exactly which rewrite rules to apply at each step. It is a
176--- powerful tool for structuring proofs, and is often more readable than long
177--- `rw` chains.
178-
179--- `calc` is designed to mimic the style of proofs in mathematics textbooks,
180--- which will often look something like this:
181-
182---   a + (b + c)
183---   = (a + b) + c        ...   [by associativity of addition]
184---   = (b + a) + c        ...   [by commutativity of addition]
185---   = b + (a + c)        ...   [by associativity of addition]
186-
187--- Note how we can see each intermediate step of this proof when we look at it
188--- this way. Let's look at how we might prove this theorem (i.e., that
189--- `a + (b + c) = b + (a + c)`) in Lean.
190-
191--- First, a proof in the style we already know.
192-
193-theorem add_swap (a b c : Nat) : a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) := by
194-  rw [← Nat.add_assoc, Nat.add_comm a b, Nat.add_assoc]
195-
196--- Here we present the same theorem, written with `calc`. Note how each
197--- intermediate goal is visible in the source.
198-
199-theorem add_swap' (a b c : Nat) : a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) := by
200-  calc a + (b + c) /- one side of the goal is the argument to `calc`... -/
201-    /- ... and each subsequent line is a transformation, with a tactic. -/
202-    a + (b + c) = (a + b) + c := by rw [Nat.add_assoc]
203-    (a + b) + c = (b + a) + c := by rw [Nat.add_comm a b]
204-    /- once a line matches the other side of the equality in the main goal
205-       (in this case `(b + (a + c)`), the calc tactic succeeds. -/
206-    (b + a) + c = b + (a + c) := by rw [Nat.add_assoc]
207-
208--- We can also write the proof like this to be a bit more concise:
209-
210-theorem add_swap'' (a b c : Nat) : a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) := by
211-  calc a + (b + c)
212-    _ = (a + b) + c := by rw [Nat.add_assoc]
213-    _ = (b + a) + c := by rw [Nat.add_comm a b]
214-    _ = b + (a + c) := by rw [Nat.add_assoc]
215-
216--- Whereas before, the left-hand side of each equality in the `calc` tactic
217--- was repeated from the right-hand side of the previous one, we can replace
218--- the left-hand side entirely with an `_`. Now our Lean proof looks quite a
219--- bit like the textbook one we saw earlier!
220-
221--- ### Exercise (1 star): succ_mul_succ ⭐
222-
223-theorem succ_mul_succ (n m : Nat) :
224-    (n + 1) * (m + 1) = n * m + n + m + 1 := by
225-  rw [Nat.add_mul, Nat.one_mul, Nat.mul_add, Nat.mul_one, ← Nat.add_assoc]
226-
227--- Given this proof with `rw`, rewrite it with `calc`. Reminder that you can
228--- use `rw?` to find appropriate rules to rewrite by.
229-
230-theorem succ_mul_succ' (n m : Nat) :
231-    (n + 1) * (m + 1) = n * m + n + m + 1 := by
232-  sorry
233-
234--- If you prefer `rw` to `calc`, that's fine! Each has particular uses, and
235--- both will be tools in your ever-growing toolbox of tactics.
236-
237--- ## Definitional simplification: `dsimp`
238-
239--- Often, rather than rewriting by a known equation like
240-
241--- `n + succ m = succ (n + m)` using `rw [add_succ]`,
242-
243--- we just want to simplify the function (here `add`) automatically when we
244--- can.
245-
246--- The `dsimp` tactic ("definitionally simplify") unfolds definitions and
247--- performs definitional simplifications. You can give it hints in square
248--- brackets: `dsimp [f]` tells it to unfold the definition of `f`. You can
249--- also simplify a hypothesis `h` in the context by writing
250--- `dsimp [...] at h`. `dsimp` will also close goals by `rfl` when possible.
251-
252-def square (n : Nat) : Nat := n * n
253-
254-def triple (n : Nat) : Nat := n + n + n
255-
256--- When the goal depends on a fact about an unknown value, `rfl` fails. Here,
257--- `dsimp` makes progress, exposing a goal the fact can close.
258-
259-example (n m : Nat) (h : n + n = m) : triple n = m + n := by
260-  -- rfl will not work here!
261-  dsimp [triple]
262-  /- The goal can now be rewritten by `h`. -/
263-  rw [h]
264-
265--- As we have seen, `rw` can also unfold definitions. In this example, either
266--- style is fine: use `dsimp [triple]` when you want to emphasize definitional
267--- simplification, or `rw [triple, h]` when the proof is just a sequence of
268--- rewrites.
269-
270-example (n m : Nat) (h : n + n = m) : triple n = m + n := by
271-  /- `rw [triple]` unfolds `triple n`. -/
272-  rw [triple, h]
273-
274--- ### Exercise (2 stars): dsimp1 ⭐⭐
275-
276--- Complete this proof, using `dsimp` or `rw` as appropriate.
277-
278-example (n m : Nat) (h : m = n) : triple m = n + (n + n) := by
279-  sorry
280-
281--- `dsimp at h` also works on hypotheses, which rfl can't touch.
282-
283-example (n : Nat) (h : square n = 16) : n * n = 16 := by
284-  dsimp [square] at h
285-  exact h
286-
287--- Aside: `rw [...] at h` also works on hypotheses too, as does `rw? at h`
288-
289-example (n m : Nat) (h : 2 * n = m * 2) : n + n = m + m := by
290-  rw [Nat.mul_comm, Nat.mul_two, Nat.mul_two] at h
291-  exact h
292-
293--- `dsimp` also takes definitional steps such as `+ 0`, so it can finish goals
294--- that rfl would close.
295-
296-example (n : Nat) : square n + 0 = n * n := by
297-  dsimp [square]
298-
299--- Like `rw` and `exact`, `dsimp` also has a `?` version that searches for
300--- functions to simplify by. Many Lean tactics have `?` versions; try it out
301--- if you are unsure.
302-

304---     Hard pointer needed to this section once we versify. Also, we may want
305---     a pointer to where we introduce `simp` (and *maybe* `grind` in the next
306---     volume).
307-
308--- ### A New Step Towards Automation
309-
310--- In the section on `Irreducibility, Rewriting, and Proof
311--- Engineering` of
312--- `Basics.lean`, we hinted at introducing more automated tactics than
313--- `rewrite` for writing proofs. The first of these is `dsimp`: by using
314--- `dsimp`, we allow Lean to introduce a small amount of its own automatic
315--- reasoning using other basic tactics like `rfl`. If you're ever confused by
316--- what `dsimp` is doing, don't be afraid to switch back to `rewrite` to
317--- examine what's going on.
318-
319--- Later in this volume, we will introduce the more powerful automated tactic
320--- `simp`, which can sometimes solve complex goals by itself and is
321--- accordingly extremely common in real-world Lean developments.
322-
323--- But, using this tactic now does not help (in fact, it hurts!) the process
324--- of learning logical reasoning, formal theorem proving, and Lean.
325--- Additionally, real Lean programmers are careful when using automation: it
326--- can hurt the readability of a proof, and real-world Lean is often used to
327--- *communicate* a result as much as to prove it. We will continue to use only
328--- simple tactics, like `dsimp` and `rw`, for most of this volume so that you
329--- have a firm grasp of both the logic behind the proofs you are writing and
330--- the ways to structure those proofs to make your logic clear.
331-
332--- ## Redefining Functions and Lemmas over Nats
333-
334--- Now that we've switched over to using Lean's standard library, we can
335--- redefine some of the functions from the last few chapters on `Nat`s. Note
336--- that, for the built-in `Nat` type, the patterns `0` and `n + 1` correspond
337--- to `zero` and `succ n`. Likewise, the pattern `n + 2` is equivalent to
338--- `n + 1 + 1`.
339-
340--- Prove some of these theorems using the techniques we've discussed this
341--- chapter.
342-
343-def Nat.even (n : Nat) :=
344-  match n with
345-  | 0     => true
346-  | 1     => false
347-  | n + 2 => even n
348-
349-def Nat.odd (n : Nat) := !(even n)
350-
351-theorem Nat.odd_def (n : Nat) : n.odd = !(n.even) := rfl
352-
353-def Nat.minustwo (n : Nat) : Nat :=
354-  match n with
355-  | 0    => 0
356-  | 1    => 0
357-  | n' + 2 => n'
358-
359-def Nat.double (n : Nat) : Nat :=
360-  match n with
361-  | 0    => 0
362-  | n' + 1 => double n' + 2
363-
364--- Note that we defined these functions in the `Nat` namespace; Lean's naming
365--- conventions advise that functions on a type should be defined in that
366--- type's namepsace in almost all circumstnaces.
367-
368--- When we define functions this way, something interesting happens to the way
369--- Lean's InfoView prints them. Take a look at the info view inside the proof
370--- of this thoerem (i.e., before the `rfl` tactic):
371-
372-theorem Nat.even_add_three (n : Nat) : even (n + 3) = even (n + 1) := by
373-  rfl
374-
375--- Instead of printing the goal the way we wrote it in the theorem statement,
376--- Lean prints `(n + 3).even = (n + 1).even`! This is an example of Lean's
377--- *field notation*, whereby Lean prints functions inside the namespace of a
378--- type *after* their first argument, separated by a `.`. At first glance,
379--- this may appear similar to how object-oriented methods work, but it's
380--- really just a syntactic variation on the normal fu8nction-application style
381--- we've seen so far. That is, `Nat.even n` and `n.even` are just different
382--- ways to write the exact same term.
383-
384--- In previous chapters we disabled this notation by putting
385--- `set_option pp.fieldNotation false` at the top of each file, but from now
386--- on we will leave it enabled, since field notation is recommended in
387--- idiomatic Lean developments.
388-
389--- As an example, observe the difference in how Lean prints the goal in the
390--- following two examples:
391-
392-example (n : Nat) : Nat.double (n + 0) = Nat.double n := by
393-  rfl
394-
395-attribute [pp_nodot] Nat.double
396-
397-example (n : Nat) : Nat.double (n + 0) = Nat.double n := by
398-  rfl
399-

403-    (n + 1).even = !(n.even) := by

428--- ## Using Code Actions to Generate Match Skeletons
429-
430--- Lean's language server can suggest *code actions*, which are small editor
431--- commands that modify the source code. In VSCode, a light-bulb icon appears
432--- on the left when a code action is available at your cursor. You can click
433--- the icon or open the code action menu with `Ctrl + .` on Windows/Linux or
434--- `Command + .` on macOS.
435-
436--- For more information, see [Lean 4 VS Code extension
437--- manual](https://github.com/leanprover/vscode-lean4/blob/master/vscode-lean4/manual/manual.md#code-actions).
438-
439--- Some code actions can generate the explicit branches needed for pattern
440--- matching. This is especially useful when working with `match` expressions,
441--- or with tactics such as `cases` and `induction`, which we saw in previous
442--- chapters.
443-
444--- Let's look at an example using `induction`.
445-
446--- For example, suppose we start with the following incomplete proof:
447-
448-sf_expect_failure
449-  theorem foo (n : Nat) : Nat.beq n n := by
450-    induction n
451-
452--- Put your cursor on `induction n` and open the code action menu. You should
453--- see "Generate an explicit pattern match for 'induction'." in the list. If
454--- you choose this action, Lean adds an explicit branch for each constructor:
455-
456-example (n : Nat) : Nat.beq n n := by
457-  induction n with
458-  | zero => sorry
459-  | succ n _ => sorry
460-
461--- This gives us basic structure of the proof without requiring us to write
462--- each branch by hand. We can then focus on proving each case.
463-
464--- One possible proof is:
465-
466-example (n : Nat) : Nat.beq n n := by
467-  induction n with
468-  | zero      => rfl
469-  | succ n ih => rw [Nat.beq, ih]
470-
471--- Note that Lean used `_` for the induction hypothesis in the generated
472--- `.succ` branch. At that point, Lean didn't know the unfinished proof would
473--- need to refer to the hypothesis. Since we use it in `rw`, we replace `_`
474--- with the name `ih`.
475-
476--- In later chapters, we will see some tactics that can make such inaccessible
477--- names available again.
478-
479--- The same trick also works for `match` expressions. For example, suppose we
480--- start with
481-
482-sf_expect_failure
483-  def isZero (n : Nat) : Bool :=
484-    match n
485-
486--- Lean can generate the missing branches:
487-
488-sf_expect_failure
489-  def isZero (n : Nat) : Bool :=
490-    match n with
491-    | 0 => _
492-    | n + 1 => _
493-
